that Bill C-282, an act to establish the Aboriginal Languages Foundation be now read a second time and referred to Legislative Committee A.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to rise today in the House to speak to my private member's bill which is basically the result of all the work done by First Nations' educators and language specialists.
Before I proceed I would like to share with the members of this House, as well as the Canadian public, the true essence of what aboriginal people are all about in an educational, social and cultural sense; that is, the gift of language we were given by our ancestors from generation to generation, indeed for hundreds and even thousands of years since these are oral traditions.
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Dene-North Slavey.]
Mr. Speaker, I just gave a brief introduction about aboriginal languages in one of the aboriginal languages. It is an Athabascan language. It is the Slavey language and it is North Slavey because I am of the North Slavey tribe, if you will.
I indicated to the people across this country that in Canada we have 53 aboriginal languages. The Dene language is one of those. Basically, many of those 53 languages were oral traditions, they were not written. How is it that today, in this institution, a European based institution, you can have a politician who still speaks this language, who can get up within the system of government and speak this language, in 1991?
I said it is a gift from one generation to the other. I learned my language from my elders. I indicated to the people across Canada that we have much to be grateful for, because our ancestors who came before us built this country. When my ancestors were building my part of the country and Canada as a whole, they did it speaking their own languages and living their own ways.

Private Members' Business
We are not who we are without our languages and our culture. When we talk about the inherent right to self-government and about building a government for ourselves, not to be contrary but to do something for ourselves that no one else has been able to do, the rudiments of that has to be our languages and our culture. That is the way it has to be.
We are not doing this to confront people. We are doing it to help ourselves and to establish something we are proud of and have been proud of for years. That is why I indicated to my people that for generations to come this gift of language has to be given to our children and our children's children. When you think about all of the things we have to consider that challenge us, like mass media, we have a lot of uphill climbing to do to save our languages.
We need help from everyone in Canada. Basically what I said was that we should be proud of our languages and proud of who we are. We should be grateful to our ancestors for having given us this gift. I most certainly am, Mr. Speaker. I think I am a better person and I am more myself. I am proud of who I am and proud to speak out as an individual because I have the gift of language. I have the gift of knowing who I am. Before I can go anywhere else and assimilate myself into some one else's culture, I know who I am. There is a tremendous amount of strength in that. That is what my people need.
My people need to rebuild their communities, their families, their identity, their culture, and if they already have that, then we need to share that. Canada, I say to you, you have to look at the context within which Canadian history has been written. You have to understand that we have to de-mythicize the idea that this is just a linguistically dual country. That is not so. Officially, because of the laws of the white man that may be so and we respect that because that is your way. However, I can tell you that the mythology has to end. In the greatest document of this country and the supreme law of this country, aboriginal people say: You have to recognize and entrench the cultural and linguistic rights of aboriginal people.
This is not saying we do not agree with the laws that exist. This is saying it is an act of respect and dignity, an
act to recognize that the aboriginal people, the first people of this country are equal and have an inherent right to speak their languages and to protect them and to preserve them.
Hence, for years before I was a politician I was involved at the grass roots in the struggle to save our aboriginal languages. In the area of teaching, when I went as a young person to Fort Franklin all the curriculum and all the material for basically unilingual aboriginal students were in a foreign culture and foreign language. I took the initiative as a young person to let those people know that their cultures, their genealogies, their histories, were important by incorporating those myself into the curriculum.
Years later I taught non-aboriginal people aboriginal languages during the evening because I think it is important that the rest of Canada recognizes and is proud of the fact that we have a country in which we are not just linguistically dual but multilingual and that we are not afraid to be competitive as many of the European countries are.
We are stuck on the whole issue of bilingualism when other competitive countries speak basically two, three or maybe four languages, and many people who are experts in the field of interpretation speak up to six or eight languages. There is no debate about that.
Basically the point of this bill is to say to Canada: "Be proud of your First Nations citizens. Be proud of your languages and recognize that if we are to take a step forward toward a renewed Canada we have to recognize the 53 aboriginal languages". We have a lot to be proud of, but we have a lot to be concerned about.
This bill is a small step in a thousand steps in a long march to some kind of victory for linguistic justice for aboriginal people. When we think about this bill, an act to establish an aboriginal languages foundation, it has some history. It was the First Nations that proposed over the years-and I worked on a policy committee with them in 1986 before I was elected-to establish an aboriginal language policy. I have some feeling for it, but I also have some understanding of the expertise of the people who forged this particular policy.


This bill has tremendous support. I want to give members of this House some information about the purpose of this private member's bill. Its purpose is to establish a foundation to facilitate the acquisition, the retention and the use of aboriginal languages that contribute to Canada's aboriginal heritage by promoting the learning of aboriginal languages and their benefit to aboriginal people and the rest of Canadians and by developing programs to improve the quality of aboriginal language instruction. Many times I have heard non-aboriginal people say that they would really like to learn an aboriginal language but that the programs were not available.
The foundation would assist in the production and dissemination of Canadian oriented materials related to the study of aboriginal languages. We are very scarce on resources in this area. It is very difficult for aboriginal people to teach their children the cultural relevance of their societies in terms of schooling-and the amount of time spent in school is a major part of any child's day-because we are still lacking resource material.
There are many things happening across this country, and I have been to different parts of this country. The area I come from, the Northwest Territories, has schools that are developing material and a language program within the education system. As well the department of culture and communications is producing materials. It has just produced a huge Slavey dictionary. A gift I was so proud to receive was a Mohawk dictionary from Mr. Ralph Brant, regional director from the Atlantic who is a Mohawk himself.
It is astounding to know the number of words and the things they mean. If we want to relate that similarly to the Dene Slavey dictionary, it is not a one-year project. This is a project that has gone one for years and years.
There is the whole issue of curriculum material. In many of the areas in Saskatchewan there are people who are working on similar projects. In B.C. the Yinka-Dene Language Institute just hosted a huge conference last month which had 1,500 people registered. The delegates there supported the idea of this aboriginal language foundation.
The chief said that the language is the heart and the minds of our people. I think many of the elders feel that way about our languages. There are few things that can be taken away from aboriginal persons that will leave them empty and void.
If I might, I would just like to read a bit from the report of the standing committee on aboriginal literacy and empowerment. We used an appropriate title: You
Private Members' Business
took my talk. In it we have what is called the song of the Eskasoni, a poem by Rita Joe entitled I lost my talk and I quote:
I lost my talk The talk you took away,
When I was a little girl at Shubenacadie School.
You snatched it away.
I speak like you I think like you I create like you
The scrambled ballad about my word.
TVvo ways I talk Both ways I say Your way is more powerful.
So, gently I offer my hand and ask,
Let me find my talk
So I can teach you about me.
There are many other things this aboriginal language foundation will do.
It will assist in the development of standards for the learning of aboriginal languages. It will conduct research into all aspects of aboriginal language. It will establish links between the foundations, universities, colleges and persons interested in the work of the foundation. It will ensure the perpetuation, revitalization, growth and protection of aboriginal languages. It will respond to the needs of each community which is in the best position for determining what is needed to ensure the survival and functional use of its languages. It will provide the funding required to enable communities to develop and control the process and activities needed to promote their languages and will undertake any other activities in furtherance of its purpose.
When one has spoken to aboriginal peoples, especially elders, one will know that they come from oral traditions. We learn our languages not from sitting down and writing about them as subjects, but from human experience.
When I was growing up in the bush, on the land with my parents and my grandmother who was a story teller, my grandmother who was the medicine woman, a healer a traditionalist and a spiritualist, we were taught the art of our language basically through her story telling skills.
You will note that we have problems reading speeches because we were taught by speech much in the way that our great story tellers told stories. Many times it is very difficult for us to come into formal sessions and relate specifically to an issue and to get to the bottom line when we relate human experiences to our languages. The derivatives of our words, how our words are made, how are names are given, are very specific to what we experience.


Private Members' Business
Let me give a couple of examples. For years I grew up with children, adults and elders whom I only knew by their Indian names. Later on in years I learned their Christian names. I went to places like Dehdeljo where I grew up, which I never really thought about as Sucker Creek.
I went to K'etsiniline, which is Birch Lake or Birch Creek-I never really knew it by that name; I still have problems with it-and Tulit'a, which is Fort Norman, where I was born. These are the names that I grew up with. My mentality was within the context of my language. I had much difficulty as a student learning English. I am not doing too badly now. Actually it is coming along. Over the years in university I had a great deal of difficulty making that transference.
The spoken word in my language is everything. The handshake was everything in the treaties. It was an act of dignity and respect that said we have a deal and this is what we agreed to. That is our world view. When we think about our whole language issue we think about the people we revere, our heroes. I think about some of the people from my ancestry whom for years I have heard about. What about a great hunter by the name of Nihtoo? Nihtoo in my language means thunder passed. What greatness is there on the earth and the land, the crispness, the newness, the immensity of this great, powerful, bristling feeling that you feel when you say Nihtoo. That is a name for a man who is a great hunter and a great leader. This is one of the people whom I come from.
What about the baby boy born in the moose-skin boat because his mother was with child and the water was so swift they could not bring him to land? When they arrived at the town the people came from the shore to the boat and brought the baby to land. That is what his name his. His name is Tahti, which means brought to land. There is greatness in that name. There is relevance in that name.
For every society and every culture we have names that mean something to us. There are many more names. There are Cree names, Algonquin names. Today as we sit here the parallel process will be kicked off in Maniwaki. The children and the elders will be able to
speak about the importance of their languages and cultures. I think that is appropriate and that is right. I think everyone should have the opportunity to say how important it is that we make an effort to protect the first languages of this country.
I am very proud to have presented this bill. I only wish that this bill could have become a votable motion. I think we should support it becoming a votable bill.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and to Minister of Multi-culturalism and Citizenship):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the House I too would like to say welcome back, Sir.
I will start with the official language my hon. colleague spoke.
[.Editor's Note: Member spoke in Dene North-Slavey.}
We missed you and we love you.
I am pleased to be taking part in debate on the hon. member's bill calling for the establishment of an aboriginal languages foundation. Certainly every member of this House appreciates the necessity of resolving aboriginal issues, and that includes measures to preserve and enrich the aboriginal languages.
When I consider the struggle of Canada's aboriginal people I have nothing but praise for the tremendous job they have done in retaining and promoting their languages. More than at any time in our history Canadians are conscious of the need to address aboriginal concerns including the need to ensure cultural survival through indigenous languages. This concern is much more than a romantic one.
My hon. friend will recall that a year ago when fiscal restraint made cuts in native programs necessary the commitment to aboriginal languages remained. We still have the native social and cultural development program which has a funding base of $1 million. The program gives priority to projects that support the retention of aboriginal languages.
More recently, in August, the Secretary of State signed an $18 million three-year agreement with the Government of the Northwest Territories to assist in preserving and protecting aboriginal languages in the territories.

At the signing the Secretary of State said, and I am quoting him here: "The survival and revitalization of aboriginal languages are integral to aboriginal people's sense of identity and continuation of their cultures. This agreement is an expression of the federal government's commitment to address issues of importance to aboriginal people and the special place they have in contemporary Canadian life".
For aboriginal languages, the agreement will give aboriginal people the kind of support they need to preserve and revive their languages as living, working languages in the home, the school and the community.
The survival and revitalization of aboriginal languages are integral to aboriginal people's sense of identity and continuation of their cultures. This agreement is an expression of the federal government's commitment to address issues of importance to aboriginal people and the special place they have in contemporary Canadian life.
Besides the agreement with the Government of the Northwest Territories, the Department of the Secretary of State has a five-year $4.25 million agreement ending in fiscal year 1992-93 with the Yukon government to ensure the revitalization and growth of eight aboriginal languages.
As well, the department provides support through initiatives of the $11.28 million Northern Native Broadcast Access Program. It serves northern aboriginal communities by producing radio and television programs in indigenous languages.
Speaking about Yukon, my colleague should listen to me because I am sure she is very interested in this issue. I was in Yukon last Saturday, two days ago, launching and promoting a book for the francophones of Yukon who live with all the native people there. This program is totally financed in co-operation with Yukon Territory and the Department of the Secretary of State of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I attended the launch, on Saturday, of this book written by francophones who work with natives in Whitehorse, Yukon. It is entitled Garden on the Roof and, in French, Un jardin sur le toit. This shows the importance of languages for this government. Mr. Speaker, as we know, 50 per cent of the costs of official languages are met by the federal government. However,
Private Members' Business
I was a pleasantly surprised to learn that in the Yukon it is different: the government share is 80 per cent. This goes to show this government's commitment which, I would say, is exceptional!
Mr. Speaker, this book, Garden on the Roof, is about francophones in the Yukon. It was written by Rene Larouche and Cecile Girard, both of whom care greatly for languages. To preserve the French language in that area is quite a feat! Mr. Speaker, I was amazed by the number of people who speak French in the Yukon. One would say that, in terms of percentage, they beat any city or province outside of Quebec and I would be the first one to bet on it. I encourage everyone to read this great book about the life of White people living with American Indians in the Yukon and the preservation of languages, particularly their native language, which I believe is a priority in this bill today.

This government is sincerely committed to preserving and enriching aboriginal languages. That commitment is very much in line with our commitment to work toward self-government for aboriginal people, a recommendation essential to discussions now taking place across the country on the renewal of the Canadian federation.
There is also the very real task of improving literacy, a most serious undertaking for aboriginal people.
When the level of literacy is low not only aboriginal people suffer personal hardship, but first nations and all Canadians are deprived of their full contribution to the economic and social life of Canada.
The federal government recognized this pressing matter a number of years ago. In the late 1980s when we held consultations in several aboriginal communities we found that no single approach to improving literacy satisfied everyone. Each community had its own needs and recommendations.
One of the results of the nation-wide consultation was the establishment of a National Literacy Secretariat within the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. I think my hon. colleagues will agree that the secretariat does a commendable job to improve the over-all level of literacy for members of the aboriginal community.


Private Members' Business
To expand on that a bit, the National Literacy Secretariat supported a number of projects directed specifically to the needs of aboriginal people. For example, in Labrador the secretariat assists the Newfoundland Community College in establishing a literacy program for Labrador Inuit. The program gives basic instruction of the Inuktitut language and is a good example of an initiative addressing a local need.
The government has been supportive of other projects as well. They are programs such as the national literacy strategy for Metis and non-status Indians. With support from the Secretary of State, the project was developed by the Metis National Council and the Gabriel Dumont Institute of Native Studies and Applied Research.
As well, the National Literacy Secretariat, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies have worked in partnership to develop the national literacy action plan that can be used in Indian communities right across Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George - Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in the short time that I have on this veiy important private member's bill we are debating in the House today.
Hopefully there may be discussions. As important an issue as this is, I think we should certainly try to make some arrangements to try to extend some debate if we can and allow members to speak to Bill C-282, this private member's bill. It is a very important bill that would help establish an aboriginal languages foundation in Canada.
I want to thank the member for Kamloops, our House leader who has certainly been having discussions on this proposed legislation, and the member for Comox-Al-berni, the Indian affairs critic who has spent a considerable amount of time on this particular issue, among others.
We support the bill. It is a very important proposal, one that would help promote and protect aboriginal languages in Canada. It is very important for anyone who represents a constituency riding that has a large number of First Nations people in it, as my own constituency
does. We must recognize just how important language is to our native people and for the development of proposals for self-government during the ongoing constitutional discussions.
It is very important because it makes up their history, their role and involvement in their life, and their participation in Canada today.
Consider that in our nation there are some 53 aboriginal languages in Canada, 50 of them endangered and some which are virtually extinct. I could not think of a more important thing for us to do in the whole question of language policy than to do whatever we can to ensure that we try to promote those languages that have formed the history of Indian peoples in Canada and the development of our country.
I would just like to read into the record the comments from the Assembly of First Nations that has obviously made some policy on this matter. I think it is important to put them into the record. I am quoting here from its declaration on aboriginal languages.
Aboriginal language is an asset to one's own education, formal and informal. Aboriginal language contributes to greater pride in the history and culture of the community, greater involvement and interest of parents in the education of their children and greater respect for elders.
Language is the principal means by which culture is accumulated, shared and transmitted from generation to generation. The key to identity and retention of culture is one's ancestral language.
I congratulate the member for Western Arctic on having worked very hard on this over the past couple of years. She visited Prince George in my riding and spoke to many different groups about this proposal. I know it has a great deal of support out there, as we say, and I hope it has the same degree of support in this House.
It is not asking for a lot. It is the proverbial one step forward, a small step forward, to try to assist with the promotion of aboriginal languages.
The bill will do a number of things including, as I mentioned earlier, the promotion of aboriginal languages and the importance of promoting that same message to all Canadians. Second, the bill will improve the quality of aboriginal language information and material. That is very important because efforts have been made by many groups in my area. I will come to that in a minute, but an example is the Yinka-Dene Language Institute which is based in Vanderhoof in my riding.


Private Members' Business
Many groups have been struggling as hard as they can to put the promotional and written materials together so that they can promote aboriginal languages. That is often difficult to do, and I certainly would think that a foundation as proposed by this bill would go a long way in assisting with the development of professional standards, of printing standards, and what have you.
It is important as well to ensure that we develop Canadian material on this. It is my understanding that there is considerable work done in the United States and other countries on aboriginal languages. I think we have a great deal more to do already in Canada, and I think this foundation would go some distance in doing it.
I mentioned earlier in my comments that the Yinka-Dene Language Institute in my riding was very relevant to the debate we are having on this bill right now. I mentioned the Yinka-Dene Language Institute which was started up in 1988. My first official duty as a newly elected member of Parliament was to go to Vanderhoof and attend the graduation ceremony of some of the elders who were being taught how to teach their language. It was a wonderful way to start off my term in office as the MP for the area. It is an honour, I think for all of us, when we have an opportunity to meet the elders, in particular, to listen to them and to hear their wise words.
I would go so far as to say: "Let us clear out the other place and put some of the elders in there. We would probably get a lot more help by putting some of the elders in the Senate than we do now from the current pack of people who are in there.
The Yinka-Dene Language Institute, which has gone some distance in preparing the resource materials that are necessary, used modem technology such as laser disks and other high-tech materials to promote and get out the information and language they have.
I should mention as well the very important contributions to the Yinka-Dene Language Institute by the Carrier-Sekani Tribal Council; the college in the area, the College of New Caledonia; various school districts; and the soon to be finished University of British Columbia in Prince George. I think it is very important that aboriginal languages, and the teaching and learning of those languages, will play an important role in the university courses and faculties.
In conclusion I want to say that our party supports this bill. The member for Kamloops has spent some time discussing this matter with the member who has proposed it. I know there have been discussions, and I hope that we can take a look at a couple of steps that might move this bill ahead.
We are certainly prepared to consider unanimous consent to allow this to be a votable bill. Second, I think we should give some opportunity to other members in this House who I know are very anxious to speak on this. We are limited by the rules of the House which we follow, but there are are many members who would like to speak on this matter. They would like to speak about the importance of aboriginal languages not just to Canada but, most important for many of us, what it means to the people in our ridings whom we represent.
I thank the member and congratulate her for the initiative she has taken on this very important bill. I thank all aboriginal groups outside this Chamber that I know have spent considerable time discussing this bill, writing letters and lobbying to try to move the issue forward. I hope government members in particular will hear our speeches today, hear our pleas, and support some initiatives to carry this forward.

Mr. Speaker, I too welcome you back after a month and a half absence due to your operations.
With too many of the 52 languages of the aboriginal peoples of Canada eroded or lost, any serious attempt to reinvigorate their languages must be worth while. I salute the member for Western Arctic on the bill, as I believe most members in the House today do as well.
Linguistic relativity emphasizes the unique role of language in relation to culture. Language is recognized as a means far more than mere communication. It is a vehicle of cultural transmission. For some renowned scholars like Benjamin Whorf language even shapes thought and emotion, determining the perception of reality. Although not identical the concepts of language and culture are inseparable. To put it more plainly, I am told by my colleague that there are numerous official languages in the Northwest Territories. That is why I understand there is excellent language harmony in the north. They can have unilingual MLAs and unilingual jurors. This growing recognition of all languages in the north is working well.

Private Members' Business
There are nine official languages in the European community. The chief quoted by my colleague has said: "Language is the heart of our culture".
You will recall, Sir, being from Edmonton, that children sent to residential schools returned home often unable to communicate with their parents and grandparents because of the loss of their aboriginal language skills and the almost total disorientation of their cultural value system. The educational system of those days did much more than to exert strong pressure on aboriginal children. Again, Sir, I remind you that our aboriginal peoples came to Canada at least 13,000 years ago. The residential schools fostered an intergenerational culture gap in aboriginal communities. Many young people have suffered from the in between feeling of not being able to fit in either their home communities or communities elsewhere.
Aboriginal peoples resented what was being done to them and tried to resist as best they could the efforts to damage their way of life. They still do and continue to do so, in Ovide Mercredi's words, "to break the psychology of domination from the two founders of the nation".
The cultural resurgence and the defence of territory are but two overt expressions of native self-determination. Other forms of resistance have included economic and political action, the reinterpretation of historical events, the formation of intertribal and interdenominational networks, and so on.
Since 1867 and earlier, aboriginal groups have actively sought recognition of their inherent right to self-government. This right was exercised thousands of years before Europeans arrived on this continent. Many believe it has never been extinguished. Certainly my party does. Claims that political structures were unknown to native people prior to contact with Europeans ignore the fact that most First Nations had complex forms of government that go back centuries. In fact, aboriginal self-government is now supported in principle by most Canadians., happily, who believe that recognizing the role of aboriginal peoples in Confederation is very important for national pride.
Canadians have a chance to demonstrate to the world that the old notions of European dominance are gone. In our country we see federalism as a way of protecting the
identity of minorities. Federalism is practised throughout the world in large measure to provide and respect the identity of minority regions and peoples.
The encouragement of cultural development assists in preserving and strengthening aboriginal peoples integrity. A stronger sense of cultural worth would promote aboriginal self-sufficiency as one of the proclaimed goals of our country. Dependency on the other hand tends to alienate aboriginal peoples and all peoples from their traditional identity and prevents the retention of some features of traditional culture. Only with the maintenance of a distinct identity can our aboriginal peoples have the chance, as was indicated earlier by the member for the Western Arctic, of altering the wider conditions of social and economic dependency which so characterized much of their lives now.
To this end it seems to me that the importance of language retention far exceeds the magnitude of retention of other features of traditional culture. Language retention contributes to the maintenance of the boundary between the aboriginal peoples and others. As a mode of communication, it is a system of meaningful signs that represent and influence the concept of the world.
According to one critic, language retention is the cultural characteristic that best reflects current and continued cultural cohesion. It is perhaps the most distinctly ethnic activity.
I am fast running out of time and I do not want, Mr. Speaker, to be talking when this bill stands in danger of being talked out. Let me quote from the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation which asserted: "No single feature of southern culture was as profound in its effects on the Inuit way of life as television. It destroyed old habits and social behaviours. It imported new values and attitudes. It became an alternative way of life, particularly for the young".
There is an urgent need for more not less funding for native aboriginal media and aboriginal languages so that they can continue to reach aboriginal communities to provide material dealing with contemporary issues as well as traditional cultures, particularly so that they can develop children's content.


If no action is taken such as proposed here, linguists and anthropologists will mourn the passing of aboriginal languages and in consequence, aboriginal cultures. It is largely up to the aboriginal peoples themselves to decide whether it is in their interest to allow their languages to fade into disuse or to revive them. If they choose the latter, they will deserve the support of all Canadians.
I would close by again indicating my strongly felt support for the bill now before the Elouse and I hope that as was indicated by a previous member that despite what is presently likely to happen from the government side that this bill in fact will be enacted by this Parliament very soon.

Mr. Speaker, before I start my speech, perhaps I may say how happy we are that you have recovered and are now back in the chair.
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity today to speak to Bill C-282, an Act to establish the Aboriginal Languages Foundation.
At the hearings on national unity held by the Spicer Commission, Canadians clearly indicated their desire to see aboriginal issues given priority status.
When the government's constitutional proposals were tabled in September, Prime Minister Mulroney said the following: "Of the various communities whose rights need and deserve protection, the aboriginal peoples of Canada have, in my judgment, a very important claim on our attention".
Similarly, the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs told national representatives of the First Nations that constitutional reform would be impossible without a change in status for aboriginal peoples, and that any constitutional accord would require their approval.
In the same vein, the government has proposed the entrenchment of a constitutional process to address aboriginal matters and proposes to include a general justicial right to aboriginal self-government within the Canadian federation.
Private Members' Business
Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that considering the impressive contribution of aboriginal culture to the development of Canada, we have a duty to recognize in the Constitution the rights of the first people of this country.
There are 53 aboriginal languages in Canada, most of which are, to varying degrees, threatened with extinction. As a government we have a major role to play in preventing this from happening.
Last year, the Prime Minister announced Canada's commitment on four fronts: speedy settlement of land claims; improving the economic and social situation on the reserves; reform of the Indian Act; and adopting measures to respond to the concerns of aboriginal people in today's society.
Creating a royal commission on aboriginal peoples is probably one of the most promising measures in this respect. The commission will examine a broad range of issues, including economic, social and cultural aspects. In this connection, the subject of aboriginal languages is of course extremely important.
Mr. Speaker, preserving and promoting aboriginal languages is a priority for this government. At a time when we are intent on Shaping Canada's future together, we become increasingly aware of the immense contribution made by aboriginal people to the culture of this country through their art, tradition and language.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House is an important one. There are many parliamentarians wishing to speak on it. I hope, with unanimous consent of the House, we could now extend the hour for Private Members' Business until one o'clock to permit a greater and a fuller debate on this important legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree that this is a most important matter. Recognizing the nature of the government business for later today is business I believe we can move through expeditiously, we would not be in a sense reducing the government's opportunity to move legislation.


Private Members' Business
I would like to say yes, Mr. Speaker, the New Democrats would like to see it extended for an hour with the assumption that the usual rotation would occur to enable speakers for the various parties to participate.

Mr. Speaker, I am in full agreement that we should continue the debate. This is a very important, fundamental issue, not just for us as members but for all of this country that is embroiled in many of the controversial issues that hit on languages. I really feel it is important for people in this House who have something to say about this bill, and about languages in any way that they wish to portray those ideas or those concerns they have, to be able to do so within the time that will be allotted by unanimous consent.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to extend the hour until one o'clock?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we agree to extend it for one hour, but I must have some guarantee that this bill will not be votable and will not go to committee under the order of 19.96(1).

Mr. Speaker, it would be asking me to breach my ethics as a human being and as a good Canadian citizen to flap my gums for no use in this House on a bill that I think is fundamental to the well-being of 53 aboriginal linguistic groups. It is a heinous thing for this individual across the way to ask us to do. It is an insult to the Canadian public and taxpayers' moneys to waste that kind of time in the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I believe that there is not unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I really believe that the House is now considering two matters. We have in fact considered the first of those matters which was to extend by unanimous consent by an hour's time the debate on Bill C-282.
The second matter that has just been raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs is, in his terms, seeking a guarantee that the bill would not be votable. That is a guarantee that no one would give because that is entirely a matter for this Parliament
of Canada. If the full hour that we have now agreed should be further allocated for this bill is not consumed by speeches of members, then within that hour the question could be put, the bill could be voted on and referred to committee.
I do not think it is within the capacity of anyone to provide what the member has asked for.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It can be done only by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to make sure we observe the Standing Orders. If I am not mistaken, according to Standing Order 96(1), if a member speaks for one hour, in other words, if there is unanimous consent to speak for one hour, that's fine, but afterwards, if we want to go on to something else, we again need unanimous consent to be able to change the Standing Orders. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member is right.

Mr. Speaker, I used to be parliamentary secretary to the House leader on the government side.
The member cannot ask you to give an interpretation as he is asking. We will deal with the first issue which we have already decided, and if within the hour if there are no more speakers, then something might arise.
Until that occasion arises, it is a hypothetical question. I would submit that we are now into the next hour of debate for all members.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will ask the House for unanimous consent to debate until one o'clock. Is it agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Agreed and so ordered.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore for tabling this motion and my colleagues for giving their approval so that I can continue this important debate.


Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, in August the Government of Canada signed an agreement with the Government of the Northwest Territories to ensure the survival and preservation of aboriginal languages in the North. This agreement includes funding totalling $18 million, spread over three years.
The agreement follows another agreement signed six years ago, in April 1985, which included financial assistance totalling $16 million. The first agreement signed with the Northwest Territories in April 1985 produced some very definite and noteworthy results.
A study carried out in November 1990 showed that the various projects initiated as result of this funding had greatly stimulated interest in teaching and learning native aboriginal languages. The process has also promoted research and development in this area and enhanced the availability of services in aboriginal languages.
The study also mentioned that the agreement signed by the government and the Northwest Territories was a factor in the territorial government's decision to grant official status to six aboriginal languages, on the same level as English and French. In April 1990, the territorial government amended its Official Languages Act to include legal protection for aboriginal languages.
This initiative is noteworthy, since it reflects the present government's efforts to preserve aboriginal languages and culture. The government is firmly convinced that the survival of the North's languages is essential for the future quality of life of the Territories and its inhabitants.
A similar agreement was also signed by the Government of Yukon to ensure the survival and development of eight official languages, including six aboriginal languages officially recognized by this territory. Funding totalling $4.25 million will be provided over a period of five years. Mr. Speaker, these agreements reflect the extent of the government's commitment to aboriginal issues. This is not a matter of pretty speeches or empty promises. These are concrete, ambitious projects that have a tangible impact on the lives of aboriginal people.
Native languages are thus valued and therefore more respected. This has the positive effect of encouraging their use at home, in school and in the community.
Private Members' Business
Furthermore, the Department of the Secretary of State has also given concrete support to the federal government's firm commitment to preserve aboriginal languages by giving priority to language projects as part of the Native Social and Cultural Development Program.
This program, and especially its language preservation component, were evaluated in 1988. Interviews in native communities showed that the projects put forward under this program revived their feeling of belonging and improved the relations of native people with their fellow citizens. The investigation showed that language preservation projects encouraged the development of native culture.
The Department of the Secretary of State provides additional support for initiatives in this field through the Northern Native Broadcast Access Program, which serves native communities in northern regions with broadcasts in aboriginal languages.
Other departments are also making great efforts to encourage the preservation and use of aboriginal languages. I am thinking here especially of the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship which in the 1988-89 fiscal year co-sponsored 45 literacy projects to meet native people's needs specifically.
One of the projects involved Labrador Community College setting up a literacy program for the Inuit in Labrador. This program provided basic training in Inuk-titut and was an outstanding example of a local solution to a local problem.
The Department of Indian and Northern Affairs spends large sums so that native people can receive primary and secondary school education in their own language.
The government's intentions and actions on aboriginal languages need no longer be demonstrated. The facts speak for themselves.
Mr. Speaker, we all know the size of the deficit, or rather the debt, and the burden it imposes on the Canadian economy. Of course, each one of us must do our part and every new project must be thoroughly evaluated before receiving funds.


Private Members' Business
In Shaping Canada's Future Together, the government defines its position on this country's native people as follows: "It is unacceptable that Canada's first peoples, who were here for thousands of years before the arrival of European settlers, should find themselves, centuries later, among the most socially and economically disadvantaged citizens in Canada. Canada's first peoples, who were self-governing before the arrival of the settlers, want nothing more than the means to regain control of their own destiny within Canada."
It is unnecessary to point out the considerable importance of preserving aboriginal languages for the future of the First Nations.
In this spirit, we believe that the concept of the Foundation and the objectives of Bill C-282 should be supported, taking into account the restrictions to which we are all subject.
In this matter as in others, we are cooperating with the native peoples of Canada so that they can take control of their destiny, contribute to the prosperity of the country and fully benefit from it themselves as well. Diversity makes our nation rich and unity makes it strong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a privilege to speak in the House of Commons and to share ideas with my colleagues, my fellow parliamentarians.
The bill which we have under consideration now, the private member's bill of the member for Western Arctic, is an act to establish the aboriginal languages foundation. I would like to say briefly that the purpose of this bill in establishing the aboriginal languages foundation is to address a fundamentally important and historically overlooked need in this country.
Clause 4 of this bill sets out the purposes of the foundation and I think it is important just to highlight some of those. The purpose of the foundation is to facilitate throughout Canada the acquisition, retention and use of aboriginal languages that contribute to our country's aboriginal heritage. Some of the ways that this would be done would be by promoting through public education and discussion the learning of aboriginal languages and their benefit to aboriginal peoples of Canada, by providing the public with information about aboriginal language resources, and by developing programs to improve the quality of aboriginal language instruction. All of this would ensure the perpetuation, the revitalization, the growth and the protection of aboriginal languages.
The bill goes on for another 20 clauses to outline the fashion in which the foundation would work, its powers and its practices. It is very clear that Bill C-282, which was introduced here on September 20 of this year, represents a great deal of work. Clearly a lot of thought has gone into this legislation.
In noting that I would like especially to pay tribute to the MP who has introduced this bill, the member for Western Arctic. All of us who come here as MPs represent two constituencies: our own electoral district and then a broader national constituency made up of the people who share a common concern. All of us have special interests, concerns, goals or issues spreading right across the country that we try to deal with. Certainly the member for Western Arctic, the member for Wetaskiwin and other members in this House carry a very heavy responsibility in that second constituency, representing here the interests and diverse needs of Canada's aboriginal peoples.
My sister and her husband, Victoria and Douglas Billingsly, reside in the hon. member's constituency at Inuvik, and I know for a fact that even though the member is busy with this broad national issue she is also providing very constructive and positive service to her constituents. I wanted to take that moment to express from one parliamentarian to another recognition of the dual role that all of us play. In this case it has been performed in a way to give us this very interesting and timely Bill C-282.
At its core this bill is dealing with culture and with language. We do not have to think back very far in Canadian history, indeed only to the sixties, to a royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. We certainly know that the notion of biculturalism was buried in the sixties as Canada came to embrace the concept of multiculturalism, a concept that is now entrenched in the Canadian Constitution.
What about multilingualism? I remember speaking one time with the member for Provencher, Manitoba, and he explained that his father, Mr. Epp, spoke five languages, none of them among the official languages of Canada.


The member for Western Arctic referred to people in Europe speaking two or perhaps three languages. My own wife Corinne, coming from the Netherlands, speaks five languages currently and has working knowledge of two others. This is in fact the whole story of our country. It is a country of many languages, all of them important, all of them deserving to be respected. While sometimes we might despair that we are living in a country that is a land of babble, we must also recognize that we are living in a country that places extraordinarily high value on freedom of expression.
We long considered free of expression to be one of our natural rights and now additionally it is one of our entrenched rights in the Canadian Constitution. I meet a lot of people who are coming here these days from eastern Europe and Ukraine. I ask them what surprises them most about Canada. There are a lot of surprising and interesting answers, but consistently one of the answer is their surprise at discovering in Canada the vibrancy of the Ukrainian culture and the living language spoken by the one million Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
Bearing that in mind, let us think back again to that same royal commission on bilingualism and bicultural-ism. As a university student I remember reading that there was descent written to that royal commission report by Jaroslav Bohdan Rudnyckji. He said that at a time when the Ukrainian language was being suppressed in its own native country through Russification, it was very important in Canada that that language be given every opportunity to thrive, because this was one place in the world where it had great opportunity to grow.
If that was true-and I believe that it was-with respect to the Ukrainian language in Canada, how much truer, how much more important it is with respect to the languages that were first spoken by the people living here even before those of European extraction settled in these lands of the Indians.
Earlier languages, as the member for Western Arctic and other members from Edmonton and elsewhere have mentioned, are numerous in this country. Many of them were only passed on as an oral tradition.
Private Members' Business
Four years ago I read an article about a Canadian who had travelled throughout this country in the twenties, recording a number of these aboriginal languages and the particular dialects. I say "recording" and we wonder how someone could go around with a tape recorder in the twenties. It was not a tape recorder as we know it now. These were being recorded in meetings with native Canadians and the recording was done on wax cylinders.
The men, women and children who spoke those languages in this country in the twenties and thirties are now gone and the languages they spoke are now gone. The only record we have are these aging and deteriorating wax cylinders on which their almost ghost-like voices can be heard speaking yet another lost aboriginal language of Canada.
There is so much that could be said on this, yet for me that image says it all. That is why I am supporting this bill, why I congratulate the member for bringing it into the House of Commons, and why I express my hope with respect to procedure that we will find it within our wit here to support having this bill go to committee where it can be more fully discussed and brought into the public statutes of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely delighted to participate today in the debate on Bill C-282, an act to establish the aboriginal languages foundation, introduced by the hon. member for Western Arctic. I want to join with all of my colleagues in saying that we appreciate this initiative.
It is an initiative that has been under way now for some time and has the enthusiastic endorsement of First Nations peoples. I believe we ought to go even further than what we are doing to day in terms of simply extending the debate time. We should actually work to make it a votable piece of legislation. I cannot imagine anyone saying that this is not something that is of sufficient importance that should not be voted on, moved through and become law. However, we can deal with that at the appropriate moment.
I want to make it very clear that as far as we in the New Democratic Party are concerned, we would like to see this bill not only debated but voted upon and become a reality.


Private Members' Business
I suppose the reason for that is obvious. We have heard today some very eloquent speeches in support of this initiative by the hon. member for Western Arctic. I join with my colleagues in supporting those comments. This is an initiative that would promote aboriginal languages, that would improve the quality of language instruction, that would develop resource materials through research, provide additional language materials for use in various curricula and an opportunity to enhance linkages with colleges, universities and other institutes in the promotion of aboriginal languages.
Other aspects of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, obviously make the bill one we would all endorse enthusiastically. I first became knowledgeable about the need for this foundation some years ago when the Shuswap Tribal Council, on their own initiative, agreed to take the matter of cultural revitalization very seriously. Part of that building process was to save the Shuswap language and to take immediate steps so that more and more people, particularly younger people, would be introduced to the language, learn and become fluent in it.
It is interesting these days to attend various gatherings of the Shuswap people and hear the Shuswap language being used in communication, sometimes simply as a formal introduction, but more and more being used by individuals, particularly younger people, in their every day communication. Indeed, this is encouraging. I think we all appreciate that a culture without a language simply does not exist.
Language itself is the fundamental life-blood of the development of any culture. I suppose parts of our very darkest history in Canada were those periods where the aboriginal languages were almost beaten out of young people attending the various schools. They were forbidden to use their original languages in school and were made to feel as second rate or third rate citizens if they used the languages of their parents and of their ancestors.
Thank goodness that period is behind us and now we are seeing, as we have seen in the Shuswap nation, important steps being taken to develop a curriculum and new reading materials, new experience-oriented educational opportunities to once again enable, particularly young people, to feel proud of their aboriginal heritage.
Perhaps one of the aspects of this bill will also be to promote public awareness of native languages. It is a frightening prospect when you recognize that of the 53
aboriginal language groups existing in the country, only three are considered to be safe in terms of their ability to continue indefinitely into the future. Fifty languages are at risk. If those languages are at risk then it also means that those cultures are at risk. So simply the understanding of non-aboriginal people as to the importance of this particular initiative is a critical part of this particular bill.
I appreciate the hon. member's motive for doing this and the work that she and many of her colleagues, aboriginal people in this House, have made to bring this light to the public consciousness generally.
I want to acknowledge the leadership role played by a number of individuals in my own constituency, and I refer specifically to people like Chief Manny Jules, Ron Ignace, Nathan Matthew. I suppose it is not fair to name just a few when there are so many people that have been involved on a very personal level in the development of curriculum and the local native languages and the various dialects.
I think it is important that we acknowledge the work being done by so many people across the country to enhance the status of aboriginal languages generally.
I suppose it now becomes evident and obvious to everyone the need for a foundation. That is why I think it is important that we put our collective minds together to see how we can advance this particular bill simply beyond the debate stage. The comments I have heard today from literally all sides of the House would indicate strong support by all of those who have spoken, and I believe that those who have spoken on behalf of their various caucuses are doing just that; that no caucus would say there is not a need for this foundation, that we have taken large steps over the years in terms of support for bilingualism and biculturalism and more recently in recent decades multiculturalism.
But this, of course, goes far beyond that in acknowledging those people who have been in this part of the world for tens of thousands of years. I cannot think of a better year to do that, when we are hearing and reading in the media so much about the role of Christopher Columbus and the discovery of America, when in fact we acknowledge the fact that tens of thousands of people had lived here for tens of thousands of years before Christopher Columbus even thought about setting sail for some place unknown west of Europe.


Again, if there is a moment in history that would require us to act it is now. The need is evident. The bill before us is a thoughtful initiative and identifies all of the necessary steps that ought to be taken immediately. For that reason I want to say that we should all work to ensure that this becomes a votable piece of legislation and soon becomes a bill that this Parliament will pass so that we can actually see not only a debate around the necessity of such a foundation, but the initiative coming to reality and seeing the foundation itself struck as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I too appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-82, an act to establish the aboriginal languages foundation. I want to compliment my colleague from Western Arctic for continuing to advance the cause of this particular part of aboriginal culture in this country.
This bill, for me, is not just about language, it is about the value system in this country. Since 1971, when the Multicultural Act was proclaimed in this House, we have continued to talk about the fact that no culture is less than or greater than another culture. But it seems to me, as we have advanced that debate, we have not given the time or the focus to our founding peoples, to our first peoples, to our first nations.
I see in my own riding that in particular the Greek community has access to all of the cultural or the heritage language programs that they need and require. I see that in the Italian and the Chinese communities. We too have an urban native Indian council in our community and they do not share in that opportunity which the other cultures have. Somehow we overlook the fact that in our major urban centres we also have communities from the north. Some of our native peoples live in urban areas and in my opinion they are always sort of shunted to the side. It is only recently, as the country has begun to develop a focus on environmental issues that we as a nation have become more receptive to our native peoples. When we travel in airplanes in the north, we don't just hear French and English, we will also hear native languages on the airplanes, see it in the brochures, when we go into hotels, when we go into the north. We will see that that community naturally is sensitized to the needs
Private Members' Business
of our native peoples. We who live in the major urban areas do not seem to have that kind of sensitivity.
This bill is really a test of that fundamental issue which is before all of us as parliamentarians, and I think our colleague for Etobicoke-Lakeshore alluded to it in his remarks earlier. There are many times, and it should be all the time really, when we must have a trust factor when we talk about issues in this House. This issue is really an issue of trust. We are constantly tested in this House as to what kind of actions increase the trust factor and what kinds of actions diminish it. When we talk about an issue like this today, it is a test for all Canadians, not just our First Nations, in front of all peoples as to what the level of our trust is.
We can talk about being sensitive to the needs of our aboriginal peoples, but now we have an opportunity to put those words into action. As many speakers have said earlier, language is the heart of a culture. If we are going to preserve, promote and support our aboriginal culture then what better way than to show in this House today support for this aboriginal language foundation.
It is obvious to most Canadians today that Canada, as a nation, is being judged internationally by the way we treat our native peoples. If we believe that language is at the heart of the way we treat native peoples, and when we see how many of the various languages in the aboriginal community are on the verge of being extinct, and we have a very special opportunity to prevent those languages from going into extinction, it is incumbent on all of us, not just those members who live in the north, but those of us who live, as the member for Etobicoke- Lakeshore said earlier, in urban areas, to speak to this issue as well and make sure that our aboriginal peoples get the same treatment as all the other cultures that have been given special treatment over the years in this country.
It is plainly logical to me that if we can have radio stations, newspapers and special heritage language courses, it seems fundamental and logical that we set a national foundation for our aboriginal peoples which will look after the rights and concerns of all of aboriginal peoples when it comes to their basic language.


Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to the private member's legislation which is before the House this morning.
I would like to join with other members of the House, Mr. Speaker, who have welcomed you back after your brief illness and time in which you were in the hospital. You know that you carry the goodwill of every member of this House and that we are all delighted to see you back. We look forward to the joyous personality and good humour that you bring not only to the Chair but to the entire House of Commons. So we do welcome you with those few words of greeting and hope that you will be completely recovered and back on the job in the months and years ahead.
The aboriginal languages foundation bill, which is sponsored by the hon. member for Western Arctic, is a very important bill. I thought that she spoke especially eloquently and especially sensitively to the whole question of language and culture.
It is especially fragile in the case of aboriginal languages because as she said these were languages used historically and many still are. They do not always have the written component to the language. If it is lost, it is lost completely. I think that is the value of this particular piece of legislation through which we are trying not only to promote aboriginal languages and preserve them, as the foundation would have as one of its major purposes, but also to develop the languages and to develop teaching materials to ensure those languages can be preserved. There are a very few actually in a state in which they probably can be preserved.
I know there was a person working on a special commission in the Secretary of State's department just two or three years ago. She suggested to me that there are probably only 15 or 20 which can actually be maintained or have a written component to maintain themselves easily.
The hon. member for Western Arctic is really to be commended for bringing forward this bill this morning. It would establish an aboriginal languages foundation which would have as its several components the retention and promotion of aboriginal languages through public discussion, the learning of aboriginal languages, and the benefits to the aboriginal peoples of Canada. It
proposes as well providing the public with information about aboriginal languages and resources. It proposes developing programs to improve the quality of aboriginal language instruction. It suggests that this foundation would have as one of its purposes a program to assist in the production and dissemination of Canadian oriented materials related to the study of aboriginal languages and to assist in establishing standards for those languages of an aboriginal nature. It also would conduct research. If a language is not written and the language is often maintained only by the elders, it is not as if we can immediately promote it and develop it without a considerable amount of research being carried out.
It also proposes the establishing of scholarly and professional links among the foundation, universities, colleges and other organizations, and persons interested in the foundation's work. It is proposed that there be a major new aboriginal college, for instance, a national college at the Algoma University College in Sault Ste. Marie. If that college is fully developed and established, this foundation could be an important national agency which could assist it in ways of promotion, development and research or could just assist that new college at the Algoma University College.
I guess my overriding interest in this topic this morning is not only that we have some 13 Indian bands in the Algoma federal riding stretching from Batchawana on the Lake Superior shore down to Killamey near Georgian Bay and involving some half dozen Indian bands on Manitoulin Island, but as well another half dozen or so along the north shore. The North Shore Tribal Council involves all those bands along the north shore of Lake Huron.
I think we are especially fortunate in our area in that we have in Manitoulin the Ojibway Cultural Foundation which has been doing many of the things that this new national foundation would do. It promotes the use and development of educational programs and educational materials for the Ojibway language. It assists in all kinds of programs in the aboriginal community for art, culture and language.
We are very fortunate in that the bands throughout the Algoma-Manitoulin area have banded together to establish the Ojibway Cultural Foundation and provided their encouragement and their support. It has been especially useful in teaching the aboriginal languages of our area and promoting the whole linguistics, art and culture.


As the hon. member for Western Arctic said, if you take away the language you almost take away the soul of the aboriginal people. If you cannot speak, if you cannot articulate, if you do not have pride in your culture, in your heritage and in the way that people express themselves or think about their elders, their ancestors or their whole culture, if you lose the ability to articulate that and speak, you really lose the whole being for those communities and those individuals.
I hope that the government will not talk out this foundation or vote it down. I hope it will allow the bill to go the to standing committee. In that way it will be able to see the value in establishing this foundation.
I would say the Ojibway Cultural Foundation has a really outstanding director, Mary-Lou Fox, who has been the director there for many years. She is a very talented, excellent person who single-handedly kept that organization going. She has kept the band councils of the area working with her and has kept them advised. She has an advisory board and a board of directors.
We are one of the few areas in the country with several hundred bands that has that kind of foundation. A national foundation would not only provide support and back-up for local regional aboriginal and cultural foundations but would assist in establishing new ones in areas where the population is too small to have the kind of organization as we have in the Ojibway Cultural Foundation and West Bay Reserve in Manitoulin Island.
The key here is that we want to see this foundation established. It is really late in the game. We should have done this some time ago, but clearly doing it now can mean that some of those objectives can be reached, the objectives of conducting research, establishing relationships with universities and colleges of higher learning, perpetuating and revitalizing growth and protection of aboriginal languages, responding to the needs of aboriginal communities, and providing the funding required to enable communities to have those aboriginal languages and cultures preserved.
I do not want to spend a lot of time but just to indicate my support. I want to compliment the hon. member for
Private Members' Business
Western Arctic in bringing forward this bill. Obviously she has done a great deal of work on Bill C-282 respecting the aboriginal languages foundation. It certainly has a great deal to offer in perpetuating, maintaining and promoting aboriginal languages and aboriginal culture in this country. It really promotes and recognizes a way for the House of Commons and Senate hopefully to express our commitment to the aboriginal peoples, the First Nations of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my colleagues in congratulating you and welcoming you back in your House. We are extremely happy to see you back in such a great shape. You bring some sort of personal warmth to this place and it gives me pleasure to mention this.
Mr. Speaker, it is with both humility and great pride that I take part in this debate on Bill C-282 put forward by our colleague from Western Arctic.
Mr. Speaker, many members, in fact most of us have read this bill and it is obvious that we each want to speak in support of it.
When you look at its purpose, this bill does the Parliament of Canada, as well as this social reality of our beautiful country, great credit. It talks about promotion, providing information, developing programs, assisting in the production, with each new item reinforcing and providing new ways of making Canada what it is, different from any other country and of course from our neighbour to the south.
As President of the Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship, I also have the duty and the pleasure to look at this matter and participate in the debate. Mr. Speaker, as some members pointed out, this bill deals with the very fabric of our nation. Parliament and its members are asked to consider, work on and pass a bill which ensures that every Canadian citizen has the pleasure and privilege of reverting to his or her mother tongue and thus rediscover, if they were lost or not as lively as they could be, his or her roots and integrity.


Private Members' Business
The mother tongue, Mr. Speaker, is not only a symbol. It is also a social reality, but even more so a psychological reality. The child starts learning on his mother's lap how to grow up into an adult, to develop, to grow richer with a full scale of values and these, of course, will be transmitted through language.
I think that the mother tongue is the noblest symbol and reflection of our lives in our society. Language is associated to the first cries, the first laughs and words of a child, as he or she starts to develop, to relate with their environment, their country. The loss of this language would necessarily mean the loss of part of their roots and it could take them several years of efforts to regain that sense of belonging, of wholeness fundamental to any nation.
For a number of weeks now, Mr. Speaker, I have been wondering about a couple of concepts. The first one is the concept of national unity which I relate to the concern for and the concept of national identity.
And I wonder whether we can find several national identities through this same unity. I found an article by Claude Levi-Strauss and Didier Eribon in last January's issue of L'Actualite, and I would like to tell you about it.
Levi-Strauss wrote: "It is better that cultures remain diverse or that they renew themselves through diversity. However, one must be willing to pay the price: namely, that cultures linked to a particular lifestyle or value system must protect their distinctive characteristics; such a situation is healthy, and not at all, as some would have us believe, pathological. Each culture evolves through a process of give and take with other cultures. However, each culture must offer some resistance; otherwise, it would soon have nothing of its own to give in return."
Mr. Speaker, Levi-Strauss is not just anybody- my colleague is laughing at that and that makes me relax a bit because these issues concern me very deeply. As I was saying, Levi-Strauss is not just anybody: He is certainly a first-class author.
Following what I was reading, I wrote that, for a number of years now, this question of unity, this question of identity, is a source of concern within organizations and businesses. And, without going back too far, it is interesting to note that the second industrial revolution prepared industry to have to deal with the problem. Companies were growing and expanding and the craftsman was forced more and more to fit into a larger entity
and risked losing his identity. Pretty soon after this second revolution, there came this author, Fayol, and this philosophy of the Protestant ethic, that emphasized unity of command and organizational unity. Therefore, the individual, caught in this organization's tentacles, would often wonder whether he was losing his identity.
Then came McLuhan and other authors from sociology and psychology. They examined this issue with a much more scientific approach, so that in the 1950s William White came out with a book and a theory called "The Organization Man". White told us that workers suppressed their identity. The greater the proliferation of organizations, the more important it is for the individual to find reference points and deep roots. Mr. Speaker, as you know, it is through language, the mother tongue, that a culture can regain its roots and be reborn. That is why, as committee chairman, and also because our minister, who is responsible for multiculturalism, allocates money, but more importantly, implements a philosophy to protect all these cultural assets.
Mr. Speaker, I understand my time is up.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know that we are running out of time. Because of the importance of this bill to all Canadians and to the country, I would like to seek unanimous consent of the House to refer it to committee, to make it a votable bill.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to rise in support of the bill. Coming from a city riding and being very active in the debates of last year when we proposed and passed a bill setting up a Heritage Language Foundation, it seems this bill is a logical extension of the philosophy that was expounded by a bill only last year.
In the context of a multicultural society which recognizes that only through language can culture and traditions be maintained and engendered and can a sense of history and belonging in this country come about, this bill makes much sense.


It also makes enormous sense in the context of the constitutional debates that have been generated over the course of this last month wherein all parties acknowledged the fact that we should underscore the importance of aboriginal self-determination. We can only ensure that self-determination has meaning if we acknowledge that people have a right to a sense of being that is expressed through a language medium and recognizes their own particular traditions, history and philosophy of life in the context of Canadian society.
I believe this bill addresses that, and I urge all members to support it.
