He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to voice my strong objections to Bill C-10 and to propose amendments which I feel will help alleviate the adverse impact this bill will have not only on consumers of tobacco products, but also on producers of that product, tobacco farmers.
I want to make sure that this government fulfils the commitment to farmers that it has made time and time again in this House, to return some of this taxation to the producers in order to help alleviate the adverse impacts of increases on their industry.
In going through my amendments, Motion Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are essentially the same. They essentially reduce the amount of tax on tobacco products. I was unable to put in a motion to withdraw this tax totally because that motion would have been ruled out of order by yourself, Mr. Speaker, as was my Motion No. 4 which dealt with giving the returns of this taxation to tobacco farmers.
Let us be clear about this bill. This government has attempted to cloud the issue and to cover up the real intent of this bill. This bill is nothing but another tax grab by this government. This is not a health bill. The government certainly has the right and the responsibility to show its view on smoking and to alert Canadians to the potential health risks of smoking. This is not what is at issue here.
What is at issue here is the use of the tax system to impose an incredible burden on Canadians who supposedly, after considering these warnings, have exercised their ultimate right to choose. What is at issue here is the government's refusal to fulfil promises to assist tobacco farmers in their time of need and to help those who want to leave the industry, and to help those wishing to remain to find new markets for their product.
Why does this government always feel that the solution to its problem is always through taxation, to tax people into submission? It has a deficit problem. It is spending too much, more than it is taking in. So what has to be done? This government's solution is to tax people,
tax the little guy. Taxation is not the answer and it is surely not the answer in this case.
If the government is so concerned about stopping young people from smoking as it claims, why is it not implementing a program like the one in the United States. Students starting in the first year of schooling are educated about smoking and are actually offered certificates for completion of this non-smoking program. It seems to me that if it wanted to stop young people from smoking this would be a viable program to implement. Unfortunately the government has not done that. Instead it has gone the taxation route.
In a recent article Hubert Laframboise, a former deputy minister at Health and Welfare, said that this U.S. program would give students: "a continuous bombardment as to the ills and dangers of smoking and would be a nucleus of a smoke-free society". He said that this would be a beneficial way to stop smoking among young people. Again, instead, the taxation government over there decides to tax people to death.
I welcome any government's concern for the health of Canadians, but I think its concern should not only be limited to those matters which just fatten its own coffers.
This bill proposes a 3 per cent increase in the federal excise tax on cigarettes and, by its own estimates, it will increase the government's coffers by some $1.4 billion.
The real intent of this bill is to increase revenue. It is not for the health of Canadians. It aims to do nothing more than to take money from the pockets of ordinary Canadians. It is a regressive tax, an unfair tax, and it is an unnecessary tax.
Tobacco farmers have been equally exploited by this government. With the latest tax increase it will take $4 billion a year in tobacco taxes from the sweat and labour of our tobacco farmers. What part of this $4 billion is it planning on giving back to the industry this year? Absolutely nothing.
Tobacco farmers have endured yet another year of uncertainty and hardship. While the past crop year has been a relatively good one and quota prices seem to have stabilized a bit, there is no getting away from the fact that the long-term outlook for tobacco is not a positive one.

The decline in the demand for tobacco brought about by growing health concerns, government anti-smoking legislation and those ever increasing taxes applied to tobacco sales, has left tobacco producers in dire straits. They have been left to look for compensation, alternative markets and alternative crops.
We hear time and time again from the government side: "Why do they not find alternative crops?" I am sure most of them would like to. They would like to find an alternative crop that would make them a living, but unfortunately in these hard times for Canadian farmers tobacco farmers are no different. Their soil is not any better than the rest. They are not going to find some magical crop to take over for tobacco.
There is no question that both governments, federal and provincial, have been unfair to tobacco farmers. In many ways I believe it is the uncertainty that is hardest to take. Decisions on tax increases and compensation have been arbitrary. In fact they have been contradictory. There has been stalling. There has been a lack of real analysis and comprehensive planning for the future of our tobacco growing industry.
The result of this lack of government strategy is uncertainty, financial suffering, political cynicism and human tragedy. The tobacco farmers in my area are in no short supply of these afflictions. My communities are probably the greatest victims of a government's lack of responsibility for taxation policy. Even the slightest additional levy on one cigarette means a loss of thousands of dollars in my communities of Haldimand-Norfolk.
Last March this government stopped accepting applications for the REDUX program designed to help tobacco farmers exit the program. Now some 600 farmers in our area are on the list. Will the federal government take some of the $4 billion it alone gets out of the industry and put it back in to help compensate farmers for that? None this year went to that end.
The tobacco farmer with 18 acres produces about
45,000	pounds of dried production, of which the farmer's gross revenue before cost is $66,000. What the government takes is $4.5 billion. That is 68 times what the
Government Orders
farmer gets for his own product. The farmer then has to go and pay for the cost of producing that product. Per package the farmer's revenue is $0,073. The provincial government receives $2.31. The federal government receives $2.04. That is a tax of $4.35 alone in Ontario and the farmer gets 7.3 cents.
Since 1984, 900 farmers have abandoned the tobacco area leaving about 1,200 attempting to hang on. The transition has been very large and it has been very rapid. Nowhere has this rapid transition and displacement been felt more strongly than in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk and in the neighbouring riding of Elgin.
Traditionally it has been one of the largest tobacco growing regions in the country. I am glad the member for Elgin is here to support me today. Many farmers have lost their farms. Some have struggled to start anew with a different crop, buying different tools and equipment, learning a new crop, and usually taking a loss for the first few years; but there are only so many farmers who can find a new crop without flooding the market, and veiy few have actually succeeded.
Farmers are a vital part of the economy of Haldimand-Norfolk and of Canada. When the people of Haldimand-Norfolk suffer indeed the people of Canada suffer. The small businesses where the farmer used to buy his products suffer. The students who work on the tobacco farms suffer, and they need that money to continue their education. In fact, all Canadians suffer when farming suffers. After collecting billions of dollars each year from the labours of these hard-working farmers, the Canadian government is putting them in a situation where they cannot leave the tobacco industry without losing their farms or without losing their retirement pensions.
Even when this government had in the past allocated money to these programs the funding was woefully inadequate. I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, if you are aware that these farms are these farmers' retirement pensions and because of the slash in quota price, because of the inflictions of taxation policy, these farmers in the end are going to end up with nothing. What Canadian can go through life and suffer through trying to produce a legal product and suffer as much as tobacco farmers do.

Government Orders
For every $300 it collected from tobacco the government gave less than $1 back to farmers who produced the product and who have lost their livelihood. Now this government contents itself with stalling tactics, with the continuation of these nickel and dime programs. The Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Marketing Board has worked long and hard to receive just treatment for the tobacco farmers from the federal government. They have asked the government countless times to end the ad hoc piecemeal approach to tobacco compensation and yet now when the entire state of tobacco is uncertain, this government even refuses to give the board any indication what compensation farmers leaving the industry will receive this year.
Imagine the uncertainty and the stress this lack of government compassion is causing the stricken farmers this very minute. These farmers want nothing more than to be treated fairly.
A group of these farmers have formed together. They have formed together to sue the federal and provincial governments for their increases in taxation over the last years. What did the governments do? They challenged these farmers' rights in the court. They challenged the rights in the court because they felt they had the ultimate time, that they had the ultimate responsibility to be able to defend what compensation these farmers would receive. Quite frankly Canadian farmers and indeed tobacco farmers are upset with this government because of the taxation policies and are willing to show this government next time around why they are upset with them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to discuss at report stage Bill C-10. First of all I would like to indicate that I share a number of the concerns of my hon. colleague who has just spoken of the concern and plight of those in the tobacco production business. The tobacco farmers themselves obviously have not been treated fairly and not been given adequate support in order to move into other agricultural ventures. But that is something that we have before us, the challenge to deal with in the future, but today we are discussing the pricing of tobacco which I think is, I suppose one can say, indirectly related, but certainly not very directly related and a whole other matter.
I must say that I support Bill C-10 in these areas because I think it is fair to say that tobacco is the only legal consumer product that actually kills people when it
is used as intended. This is rather astonishing when you consider that if people actually followed the intended use of this legal product they would have a very good chance of dying prematurely. As well, they would have a good opportunity of seeing to the premature death of those who sit around them as they smoke because we all know the implications of second-hand smoke.
We are dealing with a substance that is a killer substance. If there are steps that can be taken as members of Parliament to encourage people to reduce the consumption of this particular substance or perhaps not to use it at all, I think that is in the best interests not only of those individuals but of our society generally.
I must say that Canada leads the world in tobacco control. It is regarded around the world as a leader in controlling this substance and our success in reducing tobacco consumption in this country over the past few years actually testifies to the strength of this comprehensive approach. In the three year period, between 1989 and 1991, tobacco consumption in Canada has dropped over 20 per cent. It was during the same period that Canada passed two landmark pieces of tobacco control legislation, the Tobacco Products Control Act and the Non-smokers' Health Act, imposed significant tobacco tax increases in two separate budgets, 2 cents per cigarette in 1989 and 3 cents per cigarette in 1991.
Consumption in 1991 alone, largely owing to the substantial tax increases in the 1991 federal and provincial budgets, is expected to drop by approximately 10 per cent.
When you consider, Mr. Speaker, that there has been much research done on the precise relationship between the price and demand for tobacco products, we know now without any question that for every 10 per cent increase in price consumption will drop by 4 per cent. Because young people are more price sensitive, the impact of a price increase on their consumption of tobacco is even more pronounced. For every 10 per cent increase in price, consumption by young people and teens will drop 14 per cent.
I am going to add a few figures, but they are actually quite astounding. The tax increase of 3 cents per cigarette introduced in the 1991 federal budget means that cigarette prices increased by approximately 18 per cent at the retail level. This price increase will result in a decline in consumption of between 7 and 11 per cent or in other words, 450,000 to 700,000 fewer smokers.

According to the World Health Organization, between one-quarter and one-third of all smokers will die from their tobacco use. Therefore, 450,000 to 700,000 fewer smokers means between 112,000 and 230,000 fewer tobacco caused deaths. No other single tobacco control measure could mean so many lives saved.
It is estimated that consumption among young people will drop a dramatic 25 per cent. Of course, the greatest success to be achieved by any tobacco control program is to prevent people from becoming addicted in the veiy first place. This one measure is expected to stop at least
30.000	young people, age 19 and under, from joining the tobacco market. Many thousands more will quit smoking.
In total this budget change will result in approximately
100.000	fewer teenaged smokers in our country. Because virtually all new users of tobacco products are minors, reducing smoking participation rates among teenagers will, if sustained, result in a substantial decline in the adult smoking population in future decades.
I want to also use this opportunity to refer to a private member's bill that I introduced a few weeks ago that would increase the penalty to those retailers who sell tobacco products to very young children. At the moment, Mr. Speaker, if you are a retailer and you sell tobacco products to a 10 year old, you will be levied a fine of $10 if found guilty. This might have made sense 50 years ago, but in a modern day sense to be fined $10 is hardly something that is going to encourage people to uphold the law.
My private member's bill substantially increases those penalties to what I would term as rather unscrupulous or certainly unthoughtful retailers. A recent study in my own community found that when this particular group who were concerned about young people smoking below the legal age of 16 sent 10, 12 and 13 year olds into a variety of business outlets asking to purchase cigarettes, in most cases the retailers quite wilfully sold a package of cigarettes to a 12 year old. Obviously, a 12 year old is not someone that is 16. At those ages it is pretty obvious.
Government Orders
For that reason I think it betrays a rather lackadaisical attitude at least that some people still have in terms of this particular problem, that as I said earlier while legal and used as intended will actually kill you or the likelihood is certainly there.
Although actually I do not normally support government legislation, I find myself in support of this. I only hope that there is a chance that you would consider your ruling, but I suppose you will not, on the hon. member for Winnipeg North's amendment that would permit the taxes to be directed to health programs. I think this is a useful initiative. It is a targeting of tax dollars to something we would all support. However, technically I understand the reason for your ruling and unfortunately we will not be able to deal with this. Perhaps we could find some other way of introducing this measure at a later date, but I commend the hon. member for this initiative in this particularly critical area.
It would be easy to go on at some length about the horrors of tobacco smoking and the concerns it causes, to say nothing of the incredible costs it imposes on society because of the strain it puts on our health care system. Those speeches have all been made and I think my comments today certainly sum up my feeling on this, and it is that we should not support these amendments that are being put forward by my humble colleague, but support the general intent of this legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank both my colleagues for their comments. As those who are sitting here in the House today and those watching the proceedings on television will see, there are definitely two opinions on the piece of legislation we have before us.
I would be very surprised if these amendments to this legislation had the backing of the Liberal caucus because I know many in the caucus, especially the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who has great concern in this area, support this type of activity but would, as his amendments indicated, like to see moneys earmarked for specific reasons from the moneys raised by the increase in taxes.


Government Orders
My colleague from Kamloops laid out some very important statistics, facts and figures that we are concerned about. As a matter of fact, if you look at the projections of moneys to be received from the taxation of cigarettes, we have allowed over the five-year plan for that to gradually go down. We believe that cigarette smoking will continue to decrease.
Our major concern in the health end of things are the numbers of young people who start smoking. The hon. member referred to the retailer selling to youths, and so on. He has a very good point there, there is no question about that. We are finding that especially young female teenagers are taking up the habit. They have probably been the growth industry for the cigarette manufacturers, and of course we are concerned about it. Those in the know, not the government but those outside government, tell us that these proposals in Bill C-10 will prevent 100,000 teenagers from starting to smoke. If that is the case, then the bill has in fact been very helpful.
The colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk whose amendments we are discussing today made some points and I understand his concerns. He represents tobacco farmers here in the House of Commons.
Many tobacco farmers have left the business. There has been some help for them. There has not been a refusal, as he said in his speech, to help the tobacco farmers this year. We are waiting for the Ontario government to co-operate with a program to help the tobacco farmers because it taxes as well and it has the responsibility of sharing to help tobacco farmers. We are waiting for it and he knows that. Those facts were given to him in committee and I was a little shocked when 1 heard his speech today because he slightly misrepresented the facts as they were presented to him, and I felt badly about that.
As far as educational programs in our schools are concerned, curriculum, of course, is the responsibility of provinces. The ministry of health in the federal government has a number of excellent publications regarding health care and the problem with cigarette smoking. They arc widely distributed in schools. I know there arc programs there to encourage young people to stop smoking.
The motions that my friend from Haldimand-Norfolk has proposed today, just so that people understand the magnitude of them, would reduce the taxation on a carton of cigarettes by almost $6. Four-tenths of one cent would be the increase in the taxation and not the $6 per carton the bill purports to do. That is inconsistent with the vote of this House to adopt the ways and means motion and the approval in principle given to the bill by the House of Commons at second reading.
All groups that appeared before committee, people from the field of health, the cancer institute and so on and so forth, support this bill. There is no question about it.
He said that the return to the tobacco farmers is small compared to the end price of the product, and there is no question about that. Grain farmers could probably say the same thing with some of the products they produce, although tobacco farmers' returns compared to what other farmers are finding in returns these days are substantially more than $6,000 more to the farmer. That is the average right now and is of great concern to those of us in this country.
I understand his concerns for the farmers. We share those with him, but we believe that this is a very important bill for the health of the country and to raise revenues. We do not shy away from that. Bills have to be paid.
My friend from the New Democratic Party discussed today some very accurate statistics on the health aspects of cigarette smoking. They cost a tremendous amount of money in health care to which all levels of government contribute. Therefore we have to fund that care.
It is estimated that 30,000 Canadians die each year from the result of cigarette smoking. Anyone who has lung diseases and breathing disorders-not being a medical practitioner I cannot put all the names to them but emphysema and so on-knows full well the health care costs attributed to this. We as a federal government have to pay a good share of those health costs.
All these matters come into play. I would urge that we dclcat Motions 1 to 3 in the name of my colleague and friend from Haldimand-Norfolk and that we proceed to third reading as soon as possible on this particular piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join this debate and support Bill C-10 as an effective tobacco taxation measure.
The health community and I think Canadians generally support the use of fiscal policy as an important component in the comprehensive strategy to reduce tobacco use.
Because of the direct link between the price of tobacco products and their level of consumption, tobacco tax increases are a highly effective health promotion measure. I know that from personal experience. I quit smoking when the price of cigarettes went up to 50 cents a pack and that is a few years ago, as anybody who has attempted to buy a package of cigarettes knows. It is a highly effective health promotion measure.
There is a direct link between price and consumption. As a number of people have pointed out, the young people are most price sensitive. The impact of a price increase on their consumption of tobacco is even more pronounced. That is, for every 10 per cent increase in price consumption will drop by 4 per cent. Hurray, I do not want young people to start smoking and those who have already started smoking, I want them to stop. If we have to tax cigarettes out of existence then I think that is what we should do.
As other people in the House have said the major market is young women. That is another tragedy. It is young women who become pregnant and then pass on the smoke to their infants which causes more health problems. It is a snowball effect.
No other single tobacco control measure could mean as much as a tax increase. No other measure would mean that so many lives could be saved. It is estimated that increasing tobacco taxation will cause young people to stop smoking at a rate of 25 per cent. That is terrific. I cannot understand why there are some members of the Liberal caucus who want to amend this legislation and encourage the use of tobacco.
Tobacco farmers do need support. They need support to get out of the product and to get into new crops that will promote the health of Canadians.
Critics also argue that a substantial tax increase represents an unjust infringement on the rights of smokers to consume a legal product. My colleague, the member for Kamloops, has pointed out that tobacco is the only legal consumer product that kills when used exactly as intended.
Government Orders
Once again I know from personal experience that this is true. My closest friend died 10 years ago from lung cancer, leaving three young children. She had tried to quit smoking a number of times. The smoking finally got to her and she died. Her children are now the same age as my children. They are teenagers, but those teenagers have grown up without the benefit of a wonderful woman as their mother.
There is no freedom from addiction. There is no freedom from the cardiac unit or the cancer ward. The cost to society from tobacco caused deaths and disabilities is billions of dollars every year. That does not even take into account the extraordinary cost and the lost contribution to society of the more than 35,000 Canadians who die tobacco caused deaths every year. These numbers are mind numbing: 35,000 Canadians die from tobacco caused deaths every year.
The government is to be congratulated. I would like to underline the word "congratulated". I am not accustomed to congratulating this government. It should be congratulated for understanding the important role fiscal policy plays in the comprehensive strategy to reduce tobacco use.
In the three-year period, 1989 through 1991, tobacco consumption in Canada has dropped over 20 per cent.
Once again I have a personal story. My 73-year old mother has just quit smoking. I applaud her courage in doing that at this very late stage in her life. It is not just her life, but the lives of all of us who care about her, who care about her health and want her to live many, many more years. The price of tobacco products was a partial reason for her decision to quit.
In 1991 alone consumption, largely owing to the substantial tax increases in the 1991 federal and provincial budget, is expected to drop by approximately 10 per cent. There is a direct linkage between health care costs and tobacco costs.
As a member of the New Democratic Party, the same party that is now forming the government in British Columbia where health care costs are going through the roof, any instrument we may use at the federal and provincial level to reduce health care costs and to pass along the kind of revenues that provinces need to look after the health of their citizens should be applauded. I think we in this House should applaud the government's role in using fiscal policy as an instrument for tobacco use and pass Bill C-10.

Mr. Speaker, Small Business Week starts today. Small businesses make a major contribution to the Canadian economy. In fact, in his last Budget, the Minister of Finance called small businesses the motor of Canada's economy. However, as a result of the Tory government's unsound economic policies, Mr. Speaker, the motor is not running smoothly. Small businesses are suffering as a result of the GST and the government's monetary policies.



Since the Tory government came to power, there has been a record number of bankruptcies and lay-offs in this country. In Montreal the situation is catastrophic. Since March 1990, Montreal has lost more than 17,000 jobs in the clothing industry, more than 14,000 in the hotel industry, and the list is endless. Mr. Speaker, to improve the health of small businesses in this country, we need a Liberal government.

Mr. Speaker, at noon today three very important international organizations, the World Conservation Union, the United Nations Environment Program, and the World Wide Fund for Nature, released a very important report called Caring for the Earth, a strategy for sustainable living.
This report says: "Humanity must live within the caring capacity of the earth or we deny the human future". This new book is both an analysis and a plan of action, if you like a user's guide to caring for the earth.
Caring for the Earth defines two basic requirements: to keep human activities within the earth's caring capacity and to redress the imbalances in security and opportunity between the richer and the poorer parts of the world. It is addressed in direct language to politicians, executives, business people, and citizens.
In order to achieve this, it states clearly that a global alliance is essential for success. This would involve strengthening international law, helping lower income countries, turning around the north-south financial flows, and strengthening international commitment and capacity to achieve sustainability.
You will know, Mr. Speaker, that later this afternoon you will host a reception acknowledging the importance of this publication. I urge all members to support it and to read it earnestly.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to congratulate the organizers of this weekend's national conference on male violence, and to urge all men to support the very worth-while proposals coming from this gathering.
Men make up only 48 per cent of our population, yet we are responsible for 90 per cent of the violence. For too long now we have denied this problem, keeping silent and pretending it was a woman's problem if she was beaten. It is our problem and we are the perpetrators of the violence. We must work hard to stop it.
The conference produced some very tactical proposals. They include men's organizations, lobbying on behalf of women's shelters, a national pornography boycott and changes in our schools' curriculum to eliminate sexism and stereotyping.
The women of this country live in fear of male violence. In a country such as ours, we cannot and must not allow this to continue. Now is the time for men to speak out against this violence, and to do their part to make it stop.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday British Columbians elected the highest percentage of women ever to any Canadian legislature or Parliament, 26 per cent.
It is the first time in Canadian history that more than one quarter of a legislature is made up of women members, even though women are more than half the population.
We are looking forward to better days in British Columbia. We finally have a chance to establish firm roots of equality for women. Thirty-one per cent of the governing New Democratic Party caucus are women. It is a government of women and men committed to full social, legal and economic equality for women.

We are sweeping the country, and it is about time.

Mr. Speaker, in these financially strapped times, we need creative thinking if young people are going to be able to afford to buy homes.
The Canadian Real Estate Association has been working diligently to come up with just such creative solutions. It proposed a plan where first time home buyers could have their registered retirement savings plan assume an equity share in their home.
Similar to the treatment of common stock held in an RRSP, the RRSP owned portion of the capital appreciation of the house would be taxable. Many young families may be willing to forgo the capital gains exemption on the share of their home owned by the RRSP in return for earlier home ownership and greater equity in the property.
The Real Estate Association has developed this proposal with input from industry members, financial institutions, consumers and government. I urge the Minister of Finance and his officials to give this proposal serious consideration.
Young families who are looking to buy their first home need this type of support.

Mr. Speaker, nations around the world are still deeply concerned at the internationally peace threatening conflict which is taking place in Yugoslavia.
Not only are we witnessing the horrible destruction of property and human life in Yugoslavia, but many fear that the racial tensions expressed there will spill over into other countries in the area.
Across this country, concerned Canadians are rallying to demonstrate for a peaceful resolution to the Yugoslavian conflict. In London Ontario alone, 400 demonstrated for peace in Yugoslavia this past weekend.
The Prime Minister has said that the UN must play a role. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said
that the international community must act, that we must induce Yugoslav parties to honour a cease-fire.
An embargo was suggested. Canada must not wait. It must lead the way and continually act until peace in Yugoslavia is achieved.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention an article published in Paris Match in October 1991, which is about violence, children and firearms in America.
According to the article, it is the new American disease, the biggest epidemic since AIDS. It is spreading in schools, classrooms and playgrounds. Not a single large city in the United States has been spared. According to the FBI, 2,162 children and teenagers were killed by gunshots last year, an average of six children per day. In a subway station in Greenwich Village, two 14 year-olds shot a high school student in the back to get her gold chain. In the Bronx, a 9-year old practises shooting from the window of his apartment and narrowly misses a woman in the apartment across the street. Eveiy day, statistics show the extent of the massacre. Firearms have recently become the main cause of death among young people.
Mr. Speaker, I hope these few sentences will make people think, especially those who, naively or otherwise, favour the complete absence of gun control in this country.

Mr. Speaker, if we are to say that language is about understanding one another, then today in this House the aboriginal people of Canada have been totally misunderstood and unappreciated.
The government authorities on the other side have deemed that the bill to establish an aboriginal languages foundation would be dropped from the Order Paper and not have unanimous consent to make it a votable bill.


It is serious when we realize that languages with fewer than 10 speakers in Canada are on the verge of extinction. Those with 10 to 100 speakers are extremely endangered. Out of the 53 aboriginal languages, only three languages have more than 5,000 speakers.
Could these people have not found it in their hearts to do the right thing and not to be confronted further on the constitutional end on this very vital issue?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians deserve to have all of the facts about where their country is going, so I rise today to condemn statements made in a newspaper ad this past weekend by the Canadian Labour Congress and Action Canada. The ad said this government has a high interest rate policy. That is wrong. Today's prime rate of 9 per cent is the lowest in years.
The ad blamed free trade for the loss of 300,000 jobs. Wrong again. A continent-wide recession, a natural but regrettable economic cycle was largely to blame.
The ad said this government is not interested in advancing women in the work place. Absolutely wrong. The creation of permanent, full-time jobs for women has been a priority and an accomplishment.
This is the worst kind of political advocacy advertising. It seeks to distort the facts and foster confrontation which makes Canada uncompetitive.
Finally, I am curious as to why this ad uses American spelling instead of Canadian. Has the CLC been using Bob Rae's American advertising agency?

Mr. Speaker, on Friday the government moved Abby Hoffman from her position as Director General of Sport Canada. She now has a senior planning position with Health and Welfare.
In her career so far, Abigail Hoffman has made an outstanding contribution to sport in Canada. She had a great career in track and field for Canada, qualifying three times for the Olympic finals in the 800 metres.
More important, in the last 10 years as Director General of Sport in Canada, she has shown leadership and a commitment to equality of access to sport, a
commitment to excellence in sport to a strong professional administration of sport, and to a strong federal leadership in sport.
I hope this move by the government does not signal a lack of commitment by the government to these important achievements by Abby Hoffman. We congratulate her on her achievements so far and look to even greater things in the future.

NATIONAL HOMEMAKER/HOME SUPPORT WORKER WEEK

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Home Support Canada has declared this week of October 20 to 27, 1991, National Homemaker/Home Support Worker Week.
During this time, Canadians will have an opportunity to participate in numerous activities meant to increase public awareness of the homemaker and/or home support workers role in making Canada a caring nation.
These workers all across Canada provide a variety of services in their homes to people who truly need them; teaching young parents in crisis the necessary skills effectively to operate a home or providing assistance to persons living with AIDS. Those are just two examples of the many services they provide.
The value of home support services to seniors, persons with disabilities and families in crisis really cannot be ignored. One study found that 72 per cent of Canadians over the age of 85 have disabilities while 40 per cent of those between 65 and 84 also are considered to have disabilities. Seventy-two per cent of all persons with disabilities require assistance in their households to help with their chores and meal preparation.
Home support staff and volunteers are to be congratulated for their contribution and commitment to a better way of life.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise in this House today to applaud a group of men who sponsored and held a conference this past weekend here in the nation's capital on violence, Men against Violence. It is heartening to see that these men are taking an active role in combating that problem which has darkened all our lives.

Indeed, we are approaching the anniversary of that day two years ago when a man with a gun murdered 14 women in cold blood because they were women.
Last week in a place called Killeen, Texas, another man with another gun walked in to a diner and 15 minutes later he and 22 other people were dead. Today the death toll has risen to 25. Fifteen of these victims were women.
The men at the conference this weekend undertook to help change in a fundamental way the attitudes that some of their brothers have about women. These attitudes have resulted in 40 per cent of the people in society committing 90 per cent of the violence against the rest.
The conference proposals included a commitment from those in attendance to lobby others to stop sexism, stereotyping and violence directed at women and children of all ages. Those at the conference believe that the participation of men is crucial to stopping male violence.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this House will join with me in congratulating the participants of this weekend's conference and also to join them in ending the silence.

Mr. Speaker, while gathering information to support the application of Colchester county to attract a proposed facility for federally sentenced women, we have determined some disturbing disparities which have a very negative impact on the economy of rural and small town Nova Scotia.
There are 13,000 federal employees in Nova Scotia and
10,000	of these are in the Halifax-Dartmouth area. Although Halifax-Dartmouth has only 33 per cent of the population, it has over 75 per cent of the federal government jobs. This inequity is completely out of all proportion and every effort should be made to decentralize this employment around the province.
An excellent start would be for the Solicitor General to announce that the facility for federally sentenced women would be located in Colchester county. With 70 per cent of the inmates coming from rural areas, Colchester provides an excellent location and a positive community atmosphere to reinforce women as they move back into society.
Not only is Colchester the very best place for the facility, it will begin to correct the disparity in federal government jobs in Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, this week we celebrate National Science and Technology Week. The importance of science and technology cannot be underestimated, as these fields will be Canada's passport into the next decade.
This government sponsors many excellent programs in the field of education. One which comes to mind is the Canada scholarships. This program offers a wonderful opportunity for 2,500 outstanding men and women for undergraduate studies in science and engineering.
Encouraging students to venture into the fields of science and engineering is an insurance policy for all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, four of the recipients of this year's scholarships are from the riding of Wild Rose. I am proud today to congratulate all the recipients. Diligence has its rewards.

Mr. Speaker, a week ago today the Nobel committee in Norway announced that it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar or Burma's opposition leader. While many of us who have supported the struggle of the people of Burma for democracy' and justice rejoiced at this news, it is highly probable that Ms. Suu Kyi herself is unaware that she is the recipient of this prestigious award.
Ms. Suu Kyi has been under house arrest for two years now, following a bloody crackdown by the military government against the opposition movement in Burma. Despite her detention, she successfully led her party to an overwhelming victory in national elections in May,
1990.


The Nobel committee praised Ms. Suu Kyi for her non-violent struggle for democracy and human rights and for one of the most extraordinary examples of civil courage in Asia in recent decades. It is such courage that must motivate the policies on human rights of the Government of Canada.
I call on the Prime Minister to take a leadership role in condemning the systemic, gross and continuous violations of human rights in Myanmar. I am sure all members of the House would join in congratulating Aung San Suu Kyi for her courage and leadership.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member would be happy to note that 65,000 new jobs were created last month which brought the unemployment rate down from 10.6 per cent to 10.2 per cent. I think that is really a step in the right direction.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, interest rates are going down, not going up. Interest rates are at the lowest level they have been in 13 years. The Gross Domestic Product is growing, it is not receding. The composite leading indexes are trending in the right direction. The merchandise trade is going up, not going down. The unemployment rate, as I said, is going down, not going up. Housing starts are up, not down.
With respect to the retail sales to which the hon. member referred, he is talking about August figures which were affected to a large extent by a drop of 6.1 per cent in motor vehicle sales. However, the September figures show there has been an increase in motor vehicle sales by 11.4 per cent so that is stale-dated information.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians and particularly Canada's unemployed are not impressed with this government's economic record. All is not rosy. For example, Statistics Canada just reported that retail sales fell 1.3 per cent, the biggest drop this year.
The minister's high dollar, high tax policies are driving Canadian shoppers, Canadian jobs and Canadian hopes south of the border. Will this government act today to stop this self-inflicted haemorrhaging that is hurting Canada so badly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just indicated in answer to the hon. member's question that the retail sales figures for August were lower because of the decline in automobile sales of some 6.1 per cent. In September we have shown a very important increase of 11.4 per cent in motor vehicle sales so that the data which the hon. member is referring to is really stale-dated.
I should also draw to his attention the fact that the merchandise trade balance rose $8.1 billion at an annual rate to $13.5 billion in August. That would not signal to me that we are losing trade but that we are gaining trade.
Oral Questions
In other words the trade figures are going in the right direction, just as the employment figures, just as the interest rate figures, just as the inflation figures. That is the key to sustainable development, sustainable growth at low interest rates and with price stability.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister for health. According to reports last Friday, the minister finally recognized that 600,000 people now live below the poverty line in Montreal and he said that new measures were urgently needed to halt the area's economic decline and to promote high-growth sectors.
Coincidentally, Mr. Speaker, these are the same words found in our opposition resolution of June 4.
Nevertheless, I want to ask the minister what specific new measures does he have in mind for Montreal? What in fact is he proposing for us in that city?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I am sorry but I do not read opposition resolutions.
Second, what I said last week is that I am in touch with the government of Quebec to look at the possibility of having discussions about industrial development in Montreal, tourism, and of course, forestry for all provinces. We have always admitted that there were problems in Montreal and we continue to say that. We put forward, in collaboration with the minister responsible for Montreal, a program for southwest Montreal and east Montreal which worked very well. I think that people in Montreal know that we are trying to do what should be done.
However, I believe we need collaboration with the province of Quebec. It is what we do. We need leadership; it is what we are trying to give. We believe we are coping with the problem. It is a big problem. It is a 20-year old problem. Unfortunately, he should have looked at them when he was in power, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, according to officials in Montreal, there are now 15,000 homeless people living in the streets of that city, many of whom are untrained, unemployed young people. Is the minister prepared, in his discussions with Quebec, to develop not only an economic plan for Montreal but also a social plan to help those people?

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two things: First, we co-operate with the City of Montreal as we do with all the provinces, and in this instance, with the Province of Quebec, on the sharing of social services in Quebec. Second, I think that the best way to help those people, as the hon. member knows very well, is first and foremost to try to find jobs for them.
I think that the hon. member will agree with me, particularly as regards Canadair, where the number of jobs has risen from 4,500 to 8,200 since we privatized this company. That is still the best way to create job opportunities for Montrealers and to cope with the social problems to which my hon. colleague refers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Last week the Nobel committee awarded the Nobel Peace Prize to the courageous Myanmar leader, Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been under house arrest for over two years at the hands of the brutal regime there.
Given the Prime Minister's stated commitment to human rights, I want to ask him to apply that in two concrete ways. First, will he take action to ensure that the Government of Canada, which is an 80 per cent shareholder in Petro-Canada International, stops all involvement in Myanmar. Second, will he ensure that the Minister of Agriculture, who will be visiting China later this week, will urge China in the strongest possible terms to stop its sales of arms to the repressive regime in Myanmar.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the second point, that has already been attended to. In fact, prior to coming down, I made arrangements to speak with the Minister of Agriculture, who is in Japan en route to China, on precisely some of the matters raised by my hon. friend and a few other things.
With regard to Petro-Canada International, I would have to take a look at his suggestion. I think we have
already wound that up. I may be wrong but I will check into that. My colleagues say that is correct, that it has already been wound up, and so we could not use that vehicle. It has already been done.

supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
The Prime Minister indicated earlier during Question Period that cabinet has met on a number of occasions to consider human rights considerations in granting aid and financial assistance.
I wonder if the Prime Minister would now explain how he can defend the granting by his government of a $1 billion line of credit to Iran, a country which has revolutionary guards flogging with metal cables women who refuse to wear a veil and which, according to Amnesty International is responsible for very serious violations of human rights with torture, detentions and executions?
I want to ask the Prime Minister, will he now practice what he preaches to other Commonwealth leaders and ensure that this $1 billion line of credit to Iran is not proceeded with. Will he show genuine respect for human rights, for the people of Iran?

Mr. Speaker, I am not trying in any way to be coy, but I ask my hon. friend to remember that the statement I made is in regard to the aid giving and granting capacity of Canada in regard to the international community. That is what it was limited to.
Canada has commercial relations, ongoing trade relations with many countries, even though we, from time to time, have serious disagreements with them about policies that they have at home. In 1989 there was the situation with China, by way of illustration. Do I take as a corollary of my hon. friend's suggestion that we terminate all financing of grain purchases by China from western Canada. Do we terminate it today, because we have very serious disagreements with human rights questions in the Soviet Union?
For example, in the Ukraine, prior to a few months ago, do we terminate commercial arrangements there?

What about Iran?



.

My hon. friend is now making a distinction between the Soviet Union, China and Iran. With regard to the case that was raised today by my hon. friend, I do not have to tell my hon. friend how offensive and repulsive and repugnant this kind of attitude or development is. The minister has already indicated that he is going to review this case very carefully in light of this. With regard to China, where we have had disagreements, with regard to the Soviet Union and other countries including Iran, we maintain commercial relations.
This is something we may want to review here in the House of Commons, but it remains a distinct and ongoing policy of the Government of Canada and has been for 50 years.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, I shall direct my question to the Prime Minister.
Recent German proposals to transform existing agricultural subsidies into direct income support for European farmers may pave the way for a breakthrough in the current Uruguay round negotiations, but they will raise serious questions about the future of Canada's supply management system under the GATT.
Does the government guarantee to preserve Canada's supply management system, whatever the pressures in the Uruguay round, to change existing practices?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that the position the Germans seem to be taking with respect to de-coupling agriculture support from production would lead to the conclusion that the hon. member has suggested.
The position of Canada has been very clear. It has been a position that has been developed in very close consultation with the agricultural community and with provincial governments. That has been stated over and over again, and restated by the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister for International Trade, the Minister of
Oral Questions
State for Agriculture, and Canada's position with respect to our over-all position at the GATT negotiations remains the same. That is specifically referring to article XI. We are advocating not only the clarification but the strengthening of article XI and we have a fair amount of support within the GATT community to support that position.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister knows, the massive grain subsidies in Europe and in the United States have seriously eroded the income of Canadian grain farmers. Does the government believe that it can win reductions in such grain subsidies and at the same time withstand European and American pressures to change Canada's supply management practices? Is that what the minister is saying?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the European community chooses to de-couple its agricultural support from that of production, and in other words provide income assistance rather than tying the subsidies and the incentives to production, then we will be on a pretty equal playing field. That is precisely what we have been attempting to do through the Gross Revenue Insurance Program and the Net Income Stabilization Account. These programs are not directly coupled to production, but they provide a measure of income assistance to the agricultural community. I might say that there is $1.5 billion that is going to be flowing to the agricultural community between now and Christmas, and another $1.1 billion after Christmas, in addition to the $800 million that was announced just the other day. That works out to about $40 an acre net in the hands of the agricultural community. I think that is pretty generous. I also think that it is done in a way that would-

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Again, I am asking for rail barriers at the rail crossing at Ste-wiacke, Nova Scotia. This crossing has resulted in 13 deaths and injuries over the years. For decades people have been demanding the barriers. The barrier gates were recommended by the Canadian Transport Commission 15 years ago. They still are not there.


Tributes
In September the minister indicated he might have a favourable answer shortly. Does he have that favourable answer?

Mr. Speaker, again I congratulate the member for his concern about this important problem. I want to assure him that I, too, am very concerned. I am awaiting from my officials the report that I mentioned to him earlier. As soon as I have it, I will be in contact with the member.

I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He would be aware that his fisheries aid package is getting some pretty rough reviews, particularly from the many people in Lawn and Melrose in Newfoundland and Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, who do not meet the terms and condition of the package.
The minister has also said publicly that the amounts may not be adequate. I wonder if the minister would now undertake to end the misery for those thousands of people, make some adequate funding available for the program, and redraft the program so that it can be available in time rather than in five to eight weeks from now for the people it is suppose to help. Would he redraft it and make it available now so that it can end some of that misery for them?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a $39 million program which together with the $18 million ice compensation program is the largest amount of money ever put into a catch failure or emergency situation in Atlantic Canada.
There are not thousands of people who cannot get on job creation programs. They are about to start. I checked with my colleague's department before coming into the House. Money is being transferred to the Newfoundland offices so the program can begin immediately. Liberal MPs can stop their rumour mongering and suggesting that there is no money there. They do a disservice to those people who are anxious about this.
It has been suggested in the House and on the radio that there is not sufficient money. I am advising the
House now that money is being transferred down. There is more than adequate money.
With respect to whether or not a person qualifies, the rules are generous and anyone who can show a reasonable connection to the fishery or to being a plant worker is going to be assisted, or my name is not John Carnell Crosbie.
I draw the attention of hon. members to the presence in the gallery of Mr. Petru Marculescu, Romanian Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege which relates to comments made by the Minister of Health during Question Period. The minister may not read opposition motions, but he doesn't have to brag about it.
Perhaps, but that is not a question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on two points. The first one is that I wish to withdraw the accusation I made about the Prime Minister, and I hope the House accepts my apology.

Mr. Speaker, I also rise on some sad news about the death of a former member of this House, a pioneer of the CCF Party, the Reverend Sandy Nicholson.
Reverend Nicholson served in this House for four terms. He was a Christian Socialist. He was United Church minister who left the pulpit in furthering his view of the cause of social justice.


Reverend Nicholson was the founder of one of the first co-op farming institutions in Saskatchewan. Along with an early Jewish community in Saskatchewan known as Eden Bridge, Reverend Nicholson started a parallel co-op farming institution in that province.
Reverend Nicholson was incredibly noted for his sense of humour, his tremendous capacity for kindness and being a tough bulldog of a fighter, but most of all he is best remembered for the fact that he as the minister of health in the province of Saskatchewan introduced the first socialized medical care plan in North America, against the struggle of political opposition from all the other political parties.
Today all those parties now support this socialist program. If not, you can rip up your medicare cards. Nonetheless, I want to say that his passing after 91 full years of life is a day with a touch of sadness but also with a touch of joy as he was truly a Canadian hero.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party wish to associate ourselves with the words already said about the late Sandy Nicholson.
For most of the 1940s and the 1950s Sandy Nicholson was a distinguished member of this House and a respected voice on behalf of the less fortunate in our society. Even after serving four terms in the House of Commons, Sandy Nicholson had yet to make his most notable contribution to Canadian public life and to the Canadian public policy process.
In 1960 he entered the Saskatchewan cabinet and sponsored the legislation that brought into being Canada's first medicare plan. In less than 10 years after this beginning medicare has become a national institution. What a crowning touch for a political career. Sandy Nicholson lived a long and very productive life.
We on this side of the House extend our condolences to his children, his grandchildren and his great-grandchildren.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of members of the government side of the House I am pleased to rise as well to pay tribute to Reverend Sandy Nicholson.
Government Orders
Sandy Nicholson ran in this Parliament and existed as a member of this House, as has already been said, roughly from the year 1940 through to 1957. He was successful in some four elections to the House of Commons and, as has already been mentioned, has made a tremendous contribution to the life of Canadians.
He was particularly noted for his concern for people who suffered poverty and for his active work not only in his province of Saskatchewan, but throughout the country as well.
I understand that he is survived by three children, nine grandchildren and four great-grandchildren. On behalf of members of Parliament on all sides of this House, we express to them our sorrow. Our thanks to them for having shared him with the Canadian public and the Canadian people.
Also we would like to say that he has had a tremendous impact on the country. He has had a tremendous influence on what has happened in this nation. I am sure that his friends like Stanley Knowles, who was very active in participating with Mr. Nicholson, can say with all of us that he will be missed. We are thankful for his contribution and we express to his family our sincere sympathies on his passing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's response to nine petitions.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Madam Speaker, it is an honour to present a petition on behalf of a number of constituents from Kamloops, British Columbia who are concerned about the support for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
They urge the Government of Canada to maintain full funding to enable them to fulfil their mandate adequately-

On another unrelated matter, Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36 I present a petition on behalf of residents from Little Fort, McClure, Kamloops, Clearwater, Barriere and Darfield, British Columbia.
Routine Proceedings
They are concerned about a proposal to dam the North Thompson River at Valemount in an effort to divert water into the San Diego, California area. This plan is presently with a company on the Vancouver stock exchange.
They are asking that the Government of Canada state categorically that it will not permit freshwater rivers to be dammed and diverted into the United States and state simply that Canadian rivers are not for sale.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36,1 am pleased to present to the House a petition from the First Nations of Canada on the issues of aboriginal languages, linguistic equality and the justice they hope to achieve.
First, the petitioners ask for the recognition of the 53 distinct, living and vital aboriginal languages, representing 11 linguistic families.
Furthermore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to fulfil its responsibilities to the citizens of the First Nations and aboriginal peoples in Canada by taking immediate steps to recognize the right to use, preserve and enhance aboriginal languages in the Constitution of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from residents of Joutel, Vassan, Val-d'Or and Amos, concerning preventive withdrawal. Your petitioners request that perventive withdrawal for pregnant women be made a desirable and necesary option for women in the workplace. Your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to consider, during the review of the Canada Labour Code, the deficiencies of this legislation and recognize the need to include clauses on the preventive withdrawal of pregnant women, with pay.

Madam Speaker, I have another petition which concerns firearms. Your petitioners are from Cap-aux-Meules and the iles-de-la-Madeleine, and they respectfully submit that access to firearms is a critical factor in cases of homicide, accidents and suicide. Many types of weapons readily available in Canada are not needed for legitimate purposes such as hunting and competitive shooting, and your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to pass legislation that would prohibit possession of firearms by any person with a criminal record.

Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present two petitions today: one of 119 signatures and one of 145 signatures.
They relate to the present government's polity on wage freezes in the Public Service. Again the petitioners humbly pray that this House will ask the Conservative federal government not to take away the collective bargaining rights of workers across Canada, threaten them with job losses and contracting out, interfere with conciliation and arbitration and legislate employees back to work as it has been doing on numerous occasions.
The petitioners also humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm support for free collective bargaining for Canadian workers.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to present a petition to this House on behalf of several Albertans that has been certified correct as to form and content pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The family is the cornerstone of our society. The responsibility toward family members extends beyond one generation. My grandparents contributed much to my development. My life and many others were enriched by the relationship with our grandparents and yet not all children have that opportunity. At present there is no provision in the Divorce Act or in any other federal legislation to provide a right for grandparents to have access to their grandchildren.
These petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to amend the Divorce Act of Canada to include the following provision: that in no case may the father or mother, without serious cause, place obstacles to personal relations between a child and his grandparents.

Madam Speaker, many Canadians are concerned about the growing crime in Canada and feel in danger. Canada has always been a peaceful country but there has been an increase in crime.
I have a petition from residents of Kamloops and other parts of British Columbia, and residents of my own riding in Port Moody-Coquitlam in which they pray that the government considers giving proper funding to the RCMP, a Canadian institution, so that it can fulfil its mandate and role as the only visible police force for communities across British Columbia, and remain as a viable symbol of Canadian unity and a strong force to prevent this growing crime in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I wish to raise a point of order under petitions. As you are aware, the government is required to respond to petitions that are tabled in this House.
I have before me a response dated September 16,1991, petition No. 3430255, regarding petitions relating to the back-on-track campaign for Via Rail.
The answer that the government continues to give this House is the answer prepared three years ago for a different kind of petition related to Via Rail, calling on the government not to decimate it.
I would ask the Chair to review the appropriateness of government recycling answers that really do not relate to the petitions being tabled in this House.
