speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this bill contains the legislative amendments to implement the increases in the excise tax and duties on tobacco products and the taxation of inventories of these products that were announced in the February 26, 1991, budget.
These tax measures will reinforce the government's national strategy to reduce tobacco use, a comprehensive plan designed to encourage smokers to quit and discourage other Canadians, particularly young people, from taking up smoking.
This national plan includes a wide range of initiatives in such areas as the placing of bans or restrictions on smoking in work places and common carriers under federal jurisdiction, the introduction of prominent health warnings on tobacco product packages, and health promotion and community support activities.
As part of the comprehensive strategy, we have also implemented programs to assist tobacco growers who wish to diversify or leave the industry altogether. These programs have played an important role in the orderly downsizing of the tobacco industry.

Government Orders
I might add, as a former smoker who decided to quit when cigarettes became $1 a pack back in 1979, which relatively speaking is not long ago, I can attest to the cost of the product in forcing one to quit smoking. This has a great deal to do with that.

Madam Speaker, this strategy has proved itself most effective in inducing Canadians to cut down on their smoking. Since 1986, sales in Canada of cigarettes and fine-cut tobacco have dropped by more than 20 percent. It is expected that use of tobacco products will drop again this year and next year, as a result of the tax increases under this bill.

The increases in the taxes on tobacco products include a 3 cent per cigarette or $6 per carton increase in the excise tax on cigarettes and a proportional increase in the excise levies on other tobacco products. As well, tobacco sticks will now be taxed on a per unit basis and the excise tax and duties set to equalize those in fine cut tobacco for roll-your-own cigarettes. These changes all were effective on February 27, 1991.
The bill also ensures that the tobacco tax increases are applied in a consistent manner at different trade levels by applying the excise tax increases proposed in the budget to the tobacco inventories held by wholesalers and retailers at the time the new rate takes effect. However, to simplify compliance for small and mediumsized retailers, the tax on tobacco inventories did not apply to the first 1,000 cartons on hand in the retail outlets at the beginning of February 27, 1991.
Together the changes in the taxation of tobacco will raise an estimated $1.4 billion in the 1992-92 fiscal year, declining to $980 million by the 1994-95 fiscal year. These additional revenues will make an important contribution toward restoring fiscal stability in this country.
I might point out that it is an area in which we are projecting declining revenues over the next few years because we expect that it will have a very great effect on tobacco use in this country, especially with young people. It is estimated, not by the government but by those in the health care field that this tax will prevent an additional 100,000 young people from starting to smoke.
Personally, I hope the figure is much higher, that it prevents all young people from starting to smoke.
It was a mistake that I made as a youth and one that I know had I not quit would have damaged my health because that had already started. They say there is nothing worse than a reformed anything because once reformed they love to preach. This is one already in which, although I try not to be obnoxious in my preaching, I do advise all young people never to start and those who have started to try and quit. I know how tough it is to quit because I have gone through that.
My colleague from Winnipeg North has suggested that by way of amendments we earmark where the revenue goes, how we channel the revenue. Those amendments were ruled out of order, and rightfully so. Some of the initiatives were assistance to tobacco producers, health promotion and education, as well as care for people with smoking-related illnesses.
The government has already implemented a successful strategy. I say successful because we know that tobacco consumption has dropped rather dramatically in the last few years.
Furthermore, while the government has earmarked taxes such as the goods and services tax, which by legislation will go to service the debt and eventually start paying back the debt, it is just in exceptional circumstances that we do that because the earmarking of tax revenues constrains the government's flexibility in responding to changing needs. Particularly over time, earmarking can easily result in the over or underfunding of the selected areas and, of course, we would not want to see that.
As well, a number of amendments were proposed that would have effectively rolled back the substantial tax increases contained in the bill. While the House did not adopt any of these motions, hon. members may rest assured that I have noted all their comments and will take them into account when we are considering further tax changes.
In conclusion, this is an important bill. It will raise substantial revenues which will serve to reinforce the government's plan for economic recovery, a plan designed to help achieve a strong and prosperous Canada, and it is also a key element to the government's strategy to reduce the consumption of tobacco in Canada and


protect Canadians, particularly young Canadians, from the very serious health hazards of smoking.
I encourage members of the House to give swift passage to this bill so that it may become law and we can get on with some other matters that are facing the House today.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak again on Bill C-10, an act to amend the excise tax.
When I spoke on this bill about four months ago during second reading, I indicated the importance of this bill. It is a bill to protect the health of Canadians, of smokers that they may quit smoking, and of those who have yet to learn to smoke not to start the habit.
Since four months ago when I spoke on second reading of this bill an estimated 12,800 Canadians have died from causes related to smoking. They have died from lung cancer, obstructive lung diseases, heart diseases and, shamefully, some of the victims were infants bom too weak to survive.
The newborns perished because of the tobacco chemicals that crept from the body of the mother into the body of the child while still in the mother's womb.
I am sure all Canadians, as I am, are sickened by this waste of human life. If taxes will stop some of the harm, some of the travesty of human life, then I believe in the taxes being increased on tobacco and I therefore support this bill.
But taxes without amendments specifically tailored for health and the general well-being of Canadians naturally give me some concern. I feel they represent a callousness and insincerity on the part of this government. It will not go one step further and assure Canadians that this bill is truly a bill to help stop smoking and prevent the non-smokers from starting the habit.
Hence, I see that this bill only constitutes a partial solution, a partial component, to the over-all strategy. But I support it as well because I still believe that we can persuade the government, perhaps through some other mechanisms such as writing to ministers, to earmark more funds for health.
The minister in his presentation of the bill indicated that he was against earmarking. If I may quote him, he says: "The earmarking of tax revenues constrains the government's flexibility to respond to changing needs",
Government Orders
and that over time earmarking can easily result in the over and underfunding of selected areas.
That is not a valid argument to not support earmarking. In the document produced by the Canadian Tax Foundation Charging for Public Services; A New Look At an Old Idea, there is a beautiful paragraph about earmarking. I would mention the strong argument, the two principal arguments, why we can earmark funds such as this revenue for specific programs.
The first argument that has been proposed in favour of earmarking funds, and I quote: "it provides a means in certain circumstances of implementing the benefit principle, which in turn is appealing on both equity, and especially efficiency, grounds".
I ask this government, why does it refuse to sustain the benefit principle? Why will it decline to earmark funds when it is known that by earmarking funds we can increase the efficiency of the delivery of programs and the expenditure of these revenues for targeted programs?
The second argument concerns why earmarking funds is essential and important, and I quote: "It may induce the public to support new or increased taxes on which they otherwise could not agree by linking the taxes with an expansion of some government activity which they desire".
In a real sense then, if we earmark funds we are trying to say we provide that needed link between tax revenues and government expenditures on programs. On that basis I think the argument of the government that it would not like to earmark the funds is not tenable. Canadians will see that.
One more thing, Madam Speaker. When I spoke on this bill four months ago, we realized the many benefits that would accrue when we passed this bill, despite the limitation, despite the absence of earmarking that I indicated. In fact, I believe that effective tobacco taxation is a progressive health policy for a variety of reasons. As has been indicated already, for every 10 per cent increase in price, consumption will drop by 4 per cent, particularly among price-sensitive young people where the impact of a price increase on their consumption of tobacco is even more pronounced. Hence, we can expect a drop in consumption among children and teenagers of some 14 per cent for every 10 per cent increase in price.

Government Orders
We have heard already, and I will not belabour the point, of the many deaths that have happened from smoking. I would like the House and all colleagues to support this bill.
I would also like to seize this opportunity to put on the record the many associations that support this bill so that Canadians may know them: The Canadian Association of Hospital Auxiliaries, the Canadian Association of Occupational Therapists, the Canadian Association of Pathologists, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Chiropractic Association, the Canadian Council of Cardiovascular Nurses, the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health, the Canadian Dental Association, the Canadian Home and School and Parent-Teacher Federation, the Canadian Hospital Association, the Canadian Lung Association, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nurses Association, the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, the Canadian Physiotherapy Association, the Canadian Public Health Association, the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists, the Canadian Teachers Federation, the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada, the Non-Smokers' Rights Association, Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, The Canadian Association of Optometrists, the College of Family Physicians of Canada and The United Church of Canada.
These are among the many supporters of increased taxation on cigarettes so that we can stop smoking in this country.
I may note that there are only two or three organizations that are opposed to this bill. One is the Tobacco Manufacturer's Council and the other one is an organization that is supported by the Tobacco Manufacturer's Council.
You can see that the vast, vast majority of Canadians support this bill.
I would also like to put on the record a letter from the chairman of the Health and Public Policy Committee of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, Dr. David Sackett, dated July 16 of this year, to all the ministers of health in all the provinces and territories.
Canada has begun to make progress in decreasing the toll of disability and untimely death from cigarette smoking. The tobacco companies are engaging in a campaign to discredit this progress through the smoking packet write-in campaign. We are writing to
you to indicate the need for more, not less vigour in the effort to reduce the death and disability toll from cigarette smoking. We therefore call upon you to ignore the efforts of the cigarette companies who benefit from this toll of human suffering, and to continue to support increasing efforts toward the discouragement of cigarette smoking in Canada.
My only regret this afternoon as I debate this bill is that the three amendments that I proposed and I thought would be given an opportunity for debate were ruled out of order on procedural grounds but not on the merit of my proposals.
For the benefit of those who have not seen my amendments, let me read again the thrust of my amendments. My first amendment would allow for the earmarking of funds for the prevention or treatment of illnesses related to tobacco use.
Why would the government refuse to give consent to such an amendment to be debated?
The second amendment is to earmark funds to inform the general public of the risk for human health involved in tobacco use. Again, why did we not give consent to this so that it can be fully debated in the House and thereby test the will of Parliament?
My last amendment would have been to earmark funds to help people who wish to overcome their tobacco addiction.
Smoking truly is very addictive. An addiction to tobacco is one of the strongest known, comparable only to the death grip of heroin and alcohol. I would have wished that we could have earmarked funds for cessation programs for smokers. I believe with $1.4 billion being received alone through this tax that there is no excuse not to help the people suffering the tax burden the most, the smokers.
I would like the government to help them quit instead of only milking their addiction for revenues.
In conclusion, I would just like to say that I hope all members of the House would support this bill, notwithstanding its limitations, and I further hope that the government, although we were unable to debate the amendments, would take the substance of those amendments into consideration and institute health programs to address those very issues and concerns that I hope the government equally believes are important. I hope it would support them with added funds, including the preservation of our health care system.

Madam Speaker, I want to say that I am happy to have an opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-10, a bill that essentially sees an increase in taxes on tobacco products.
I want to begin by first of all saying that I very seldom find myself agreeing with initiatives that the government has taken over the last little while, but this is one where I find myself in complete agreement. It is appropriate that we use fiscal policy in an effort to introduce a comprehensive strategy to reduce the use of tobacco.
I want to begin my comments by simply stating that tobacco, as far as I am aware, is the only legal consumer product that actually kills people when used exactly as it is intended to be used. In other words, if you smoke, there is a very good chance that you will end your life prematurely. You will have an influence on ending the lives of other people prematurely as well as a result of the second hand use of tobacco. As a matter of fact, I think the statistics would indicate that in an average year,
35,000	deaths occur in Canada directly related to the use of tobacco, to say nothing of all of those folks who find themselves spending time in cancer clinics, in cardiac wards, suffering from emphysema and other related illnesses.
Again, I think the statistics of second hand smoke indicate very clearly that smoking is something that we ought to encourage people to eliminate and certainly to reduce.
However, before getting into the subject matter itself, I want to simply say that we ought not to lose sight of the fact that 1,200 growers are involved in the tobacco industry as farmers. While we are taking steps here in Parliament in a variety of ways to encourage people not to consume tobacco, the reality is that it is a legal product and there are 1,200 families involved in its production, to say nothing of another few thousand involved in the production and sales of tobacco who
Government Orders
depend on the industry for their livelihood. There is not one in this House of Commons who would not support increased activity, increased financial support to encourage those growers to get out of the tobacco growing business and into something else that would be more acceptable to Canadian society generally.
We have made positive steps in this direction over the last number of years, but we have a lot to go.
It is interesting when you look at the price of a package of cigarettes today, and they cost about $5 or $6, depending on where you buy them, and yet the actual farmer only receives about 7 cents of that. It can be seen in terms of the amount of money consumed in taxes and in other costs throughout the system in terms of production and marketing of tobacco, 7 cents going to the farmer means that there is certainly a great deal being generated to society to say nothing of taxes.
The minister earlier indicated an interesting trend, that the government is actually projecting a decline in revenue over the next number of years as a result of this initiative. A lot of people are of the opinion that we simply keep jacking up the taxes on the price of tobacco to gain additional revenue. Well, to a point that does work.
I think we have reached the point now where the taxes and costs are so high that it is actually having an effect on the number of people smoking or beginning to smoke, so that the use is falling off and consequently the long-term revenue to government will actually decline. I think that in terms of a financial viewpoint it is probably bad news but over all we have to welcome the trend that fewer and fewer people are involved with smoking tobacco.
I might say in my constituency a lot of people chew tobacco. I tried it once, got sick and did not try it any more. Baseball players and cowboys it seems still find that to be an interesting way to consume tobacco.
I want to point out some very encouraging statistics. Let us also acknowledge the fact that Canada is a world leader in tobacco control. This Parliament has passed the Tobacco Products Control Act and the Non-smokers' Health Act which have had significant impact in seeing Canadians set aside their packs of cigarettes or their pipes or cigars or chewing tobacco and move away from that habit. In the three year period between 1989 and 1991 tobacco consumption in Canada dropped over 20 per cent. What is encouraging is the drop with young people.


Government Orders
Statistically we know that there is a very clear relationship between the price of a commodity and the demand for the commodity. It is fair to say that statistics and studies have proven that for every 10 per cent increase in price of tobacco, consumption will drop by 14 per cent. It is even more when you consider young people because they are very price sensitive. They are not as addicted, if you like, as older folks and they have less disposable income. For every 10 per cent increase in price of consumption by young people-I mean by that children and teens-the consumption does not drop 4 per cent, it actually drops 14 per cent.
We can see that this most recent round of price increases on a package of cigarettes will be encouraging younger people not to smoke even more.
We know that the tax increase of 3 cents per cigarette introduced in the 1991 federal budget means that cigarette prices increased by approximately 18 per cent at the retail level.
Let me just as an aside say something about the retail level. As a result of a recent study that was completed in my constituency of Kamloops and I suspect duplicated in other areas, I am just not aware of the various studies, people were puzzled by the seemingly ease with which young people, and I mean very young people, could purchase cigarettes.
It is illegal to sell cigarettes to someone under the age of 16. However, when you look at the act that was passed, which must have been 100 years ago, it said that if you are caught as a retailer selling cigarettes to children, you will be fined, get this, $10. Hardly a punitive sum. If you are caught twice, you get fined $25. The third time is really heavy, you get a $100 fine. Obviously what this means is that people will just ignore this and sell to children. Some retailers do not. They recognize the law for what it is, for a good reason and refuse to sell.
A study was done in Kamloops. One of the local organizations concerned about the increased amount of smoking by young people, particularly young girls, sent children to the various stores, 14, 12,11 and 10 year olds, and found that it really did not matter if you were 10, 12 or 14, a retailer sold you cigarettes. I think we all appreciate that if someone 10 years old comes in asking for a package of Rothman's, they are obviously not 16 and the retailer ought not to be selling it to them.
I have introduced a Private Members' Bill for those thoughtless retailers who sell cigarettes to children. If they are caught, the first offence would be a fine not exceeding $1,000; the second offence, $2,000; and the third offence, $5,000. Hopefully this will encourage people to simply obey the law if you are selling cigarettes to people, and particularly young people.
It is interesting that the price increase of the 1990-91 federal budget will result in a decline in consumption of between 7 per cent and 11 per cent or, in other words,
450,000	to 700,000 fewer smokers. According to the World Health Organization, between one-quarter and one-third of all smokers will die from their tobacco use. Therefore, we can extrapolate that 112,000 to 230,000 fewer tobacco caused deaths will occur as a result of these tax increases in the 1990-91 federal budget.
That is encouraging. No other single tobacco control measure could mean so many lives saved. It is estimated that consumption among young people will drop a dramatic 25 per cent as a result of this increase. The greatest success to be achieved by any tobacco control program is to prevent people from becoming addicted in the first place. This one measure is expected to stop at least 30,000 young people under the age of 19 from joining the tobacco market and many thousands more will quit smoking on top of that. In total, the assumption is that the budget increase in tobacco taxes will result in approximately 100,000 fewer teenage smokers.
That is great news. Any step that will result in 100,000 teenagers not starting to smoke has to be a welcomed initiative. I was pleased to see in the voting earlier today on this matter that it had the overwhelming support of the members of the House.
I want to refer to one rather disturbing fact that has become known in the last little while and that is the fact that the tobacco marketers are aiming at young women as a target market. It has worked because if you look to see where the increase in smoking is occurring, it is among young women. I would like to think that we will take steps as a Parliament to encourage all people, particularly young people and young women, to reconsider what they are doing, acknowledging the fact that tobacco will kill you or result certainly in a premature death.


I want to say that my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North had an interesting suggestion in his amendments. He tries to suggest that some of these increased tax revenues should go toward an educational program and to treating smokers and encouraging those who are considering smoking not to.
I noticed that the government when it collected the GST targeted some excess revenue there toward deficit reduction which in a sense is a bogus plan but, in that same kind of thinking, not the bogus part but the serious part, we should be suggesting that some of these additional revenues should go into a massive campaign to encourage young people not to smoke and not to begin smoking, which will likely result in some form of addiction.
I must say that I find it troubling to attend sporting events and often find that they are endorsed by cigarette manufacturers. Encouraging young athletes and so on to get involved in sporting activities and having to resort to the tobacco companies endorsing those athletic or sporting activities is a little odd in logic and is something that we need to consider in the future.
I want to simply add to my comments by suggesting that when people say "look at the price of tobacco products", if we actually look what happened in our country between 1950 and 1980 and just adjusting for inflation, we find that the real price of tobacco actually fell and that tobacco is actually cheaper to obtain in terms of a typical wage earner in the country now than it was years ago in spite of what appears to be an incredibly high cost for a package of tobacco. In terms of what these additional taxes have done, they have not even kept up to the rate of inflation.
In closing, I simply want to say that the fact that so much cross-border shopping is resulting now in illegal cigarettes from the United States coming to Canada is a reflection that the United States really has not appreciated this problem as we have in Canada. In the United States taxes on cigarettes account for about 27 per cent of the retail price.
Government Orders
In Canada it is closer to 67 per cent of the retail price. What we are saying is that while we have passed legislation in this Parliament to preclude smoking in federal precincts and taken steps to encourage people not to smoke, the United States has not done the same.
It is a sad fact that people find themselves going across the border to pick up cheaper priced cigarettes. It is inferior tobacco, as we all know, and inferior cigarettes. It does indicate the challenge that is before us.
In closing, I want to say that we support this legislation. We support the fact that it has proven successful in terms of increased taxing and taxes on cigarettes have resulted in a decline in use. However, let us also acknowledge that as the industry winds down, and hopefully will continue to wind down and save a lot of peoples' lives in the process, we simply cannot ignore the tobacco producers.
While we change our laws and our positioning on this particular commodity, they are in a sense the innocent bystanders. We have to acknowledge that fact and introduce clear programs that will help them in their transition to other forms of agriculture or other economic activities.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of my colleague from Kamloops on this very important issue.
There are four points that I would like to make as observations, and I am wondering if he might comment on them.
The first is that the government is taking something in the order of $60 million out of this. I got my figure confused, but it is a large amount of money. It is only part of the solution to this. There needs to be additional action taken by the government.
It has been said that in the reform of health care, probably the most critical thing that has to be done in this place and the provincial legislatures across Canada is to address driving, smoking and alcohol in the reform of the health care system because of the lifestyle problems

Government Orders
that are created in health care. This is one of the critical ones.
The House of Commons, through the office of the Speaker, could provide a very effective model across this country. I know the House provides opportunities for staff and members to participate in quit-smoking programs, but there is no rigorous attempt to sell that program. There is no attempt to assess the size of the problem, to follow up and to catch those who fall off after the initial investment is made.
The Government of Canada pays for it, but it does not do it effectively. It could be very effective. I do not think I have ever met a smoker who does not want to quit smoking.
The second thing is the government has put forward a proposal to end the partisanship nature of the House of Commons, and I could not think of a better issue than this one. I think my colleague will agree.
I have talked to many members on the government side, in the Liberal caucus and in our own caucus who want to see something positive and constructive done to bring this issue forward and to reduce smoking.
I would think that this is the kind of a situation that the committee could continue on. There needs to be a ban, as my colleague has said, on export and import of this product.
It could quickly cut down a great amount of infringement of the intent of the law if that were to happen, both exporting the product to Third World countries and allowing the imported product to beat the prohibitive nature of the cost here.
The last thing is the conversion cost for farmers and the production and distribution cycle. Those people are the innocent victims of it. The money taken in by that tax, and I know the government is reluctant to do this, should be specifically targeted into the smoking area. It should provide assistance so farmers can convert to other products and so manufacturers can orderly scale down operations and exit the business and so that workers can be relocated and retrained.
The four points are, in summary, as follows: The House of Commons should be a model of an organization that really attacks the problem of smoking by helping people to get off it, following it up and for those who want out, help them out.
As for the constitutional move to make this place non-partisan, we all agree on what should be done and I
think we should move forward as a group to end this as much as we can. Export and import, get on with targeting the conversion costs.

Madam Speaker, I would like to respond to those very thoughtful interventions by my hon. colleague.
While the House of Commons has taken a number of steps to encourage members and people that are employed on Parliament Hill not to smoke, with I think relative success, although we still find long line-ups outside the doorways with people squeezing in that last cigarette before they start or slipping out for a quick one, particularly during the winter months, which looks a little odd, but we still have some work to do and there is still much that could be done.
I remember the days when we used to have all of those ash trays out behind the curtains and everybody would be out there smoking. Now you do not find anybody out there smoking at least, and no ash trays. I think we have made tremendous progress and ought to continue to work for, as my colleague says, setting a model for what can be accomplished if we set our minds to it.
Also, the acknowledgement of my hon. friend that there is a tremendous cost associated with our health care system when you consider all of the people suffering from some aspect of smoke-related illnesses. The cost is horrendous. Therefore, it would really be an investment of significant proportions to encourage, particularly young people not to smoke. We acknowledge the fact that if you can keep a young person from smoking up until age 18 you have probably won the battle, that very few people are addicted after the age of 18. Therein lies the challenge in our school programs. I think we would all agree that really we have only touched the surface, that not a great deal has been done.
Madam Speaker, when you look at a package of cigarettes these days and see about half the pack covered with a sign saying "smoking is injurious to your health; smoking causes cancer; if you are pregnant don't smoke", and so on, you would think that people would get the clue that this is not a good idea. As my hon. friend has indicated, I think most people have. But the facts are that it is an addiction and how you rid yourself of this addiction obviously requires a major effort, and that while progress is being made much more ought to be done.

I want to thank my hon. colleague for his intervention, and particularly again his reference to the fact that transitional funds must be provided for the growers in the business. We must also re-think our export of tobacco products, particularly to the developing world. One reads with a great deal of disappointment that the major marketing now of tobacco products is into the poorest parts of the world, into the parts of the world where, since one is having difficulty selling them in Canada, that a major initiative is being taken to sell cigarette products in the developing countries. This is something we should not be encouraging, and as a matter of fact should be taking steps to eliminate.

Madam Speaker, I do not wish to belabour the point because we agree absolutely. But another suggestion is that it is ironic; in the House of Commons it is not just a matter of prohibiting people from smoking in offices, which is observed or not observed, but the House spends thousands and thousands of dollars on programs. If a member of Parliament or a staff member wishes to sign up for a non-smoking program the House will pay for it and that is a very positive move.
Unfortunately the health officials in the administration of the House do not attempt to size up the size of the problem. They do not attempt to target it or promote it. The second thing they do not do is that if somebody takes that program there is absolutely no follow-up. People here have suggested they do not have the resources to do that. But, in fact, there is a school of nursing at the University of Ottawa, in Algonquin College, where students could-probably as part of their project-do an assessment. I discussed this previously with a number of folks who thought that they would be quite prepared as a project in health care to come in here, do an assessment and do a follow-up.
But what I am arguing about is that we could set an example here. The second thing is that the House leader, in speaking to his other colleagues, might be able to approach the Speaker and ask if something slightly more energetic could be done to begin to set the model on the Hill. I know the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is a solid supporter of the kinds of activity that go in his report on health care and it is well known that the lifestyle types of things are important.
So right within the House things can be done. I would also like to say that he did not comment on the
Government Orders
non-partisan nature of the desire of the government to move into areas where members of Parliament do agree.
I am wondering about the possibility of House leaders sitting down for a discussion on what might be added to the health care committee to see whether or not the government may want to target some of these tax dollars to education programs, to conversion programs, and to really make this thing work. The government's initiative in using the stick is fine, but additionally there needs to be more on the carrot that would encourage people to get off the habit.

Madam Speaker, I am taking part in this debate today as a non-smoker. I am very proud to say that none of my children smoke either, but yet I am the first to recognize that perhaps through continuing research, partially funded by the Government of Canada, the Canadian tobacco industry has one of the best products of any country in the world. They have lower tar and nicotine content than most other countries of the world. Consequently the Canadian product itself is not only of higher quality but it is much safer.
We only have about 1,200 growers left and yet in 1988-1989 fiscal year those farmers contributed $2,097 billion in tax revenues to various levels of government in this country.
What we are seeing in this bill is another tax grab that is going to drive Canadians into more cross-border shopping to pick up cigarettes at about half the price. Of course, while they are over there they will buy other products that are cheaper because the retail sector does not take as big a mark-up and because there are not as many levels between the growers and the retail outlet. They will also fill up with gasoline, again made far more expensive by the levels of taxes in this country. This is hurting the cross-border communities in a very dramatic way.
The minister spoke earlier today about a national plan to reduce smoking. He said that the strategy would be effective to reduce this but I have to ask the question how much of this revenue has been missed not only due to the cross-border shopping but also due to the illicit trade that we are reading more and more about as time goes on. I believe that the increased taxes have had an adverse effect not only on government revenues but maintaining a desire for the people to obtain their tobacco needs in the U.S.


Government Orders
A few months ago the minister of energy, and I hope he will come back in, made a comment on a comparable product, and I would be very remiss if I did not touch on it now that he has mentioned it.
Tobacco has been described here today in the House as a legal killer. I have to suggest there is another substance used in Canada at the present time that is an insidious neurotoxic substance which is certainly banned in some other countries but is still being used here in Canada.
He looked at tobacco being labelled as a killer. I suggest that the octane enhancer currently used in gasolines in Canada, MMT, which is methylcyclopenta-dienyl manganese tricarbonyl, is nearly as bad as the product it replaced which is tetra-ethyl lead. I have documents that suggest that while we are flailing away at the tobacco industry to protect the lives of Canadian people, the sad part is that other ingredients used in our gasoline is particularly harmful to the health of infants and children. They are the most vulnerable victims of this substance, yet tobacco products are not used by these young people or children whose immune systems are not yet in place.
I would like to cite from the June issue of the Canadian Medical Journal, where it points out that among infants 10 to 14 months of age in low-income families in Montreal, 24.3 per cent had iron deficiency anaemia.
Then we look at some research done by Michael and Judy Ashner at Albany Medical College, in Albany, New York. They found that in laboratory animals that have iron deficiencies the uptake of manganese accelerates dramatically.
This happens in laboratory animals and of course the laboratory work is done to assess the impact of these substances on humans. Then does it also follow that many of these infants in Canada whose blood brain barriers are not yet in place and who do not have the mechanisms to excrete this substance may also be at risk.
Therefore, I suggest that we have a double standard here. We are aiming to eliminate smoking by imposing high taxes on the smokers, yet we are continuing to allow
the use of the substance MMT containing manganese in our automotive fuels. We are allowing MN3 to come out of the exhaust systems of cars that causes pollution and the MN3 is taken into the respiratory systems and accumulates in the bodies, not only of children who are the most susceptible, but also other Canadians. It is taken in through the respiratory system and it accumulates and attacks the cells at the base of the brain.
There is another double standard here. Tobacco is produced here in Canada, and as I indicated earlier, it has the lowest chemical content, nicotine content, of any nation in the world. But we allow the importation of a product into Canada that is not even manufactured here that places the health of our children and adults at risk.
I have to say that I am amazed that this government can bring in a tax measure such as this on the pretext of trying to force Canadians to quit smoking and at the same time allowing the continuous use of an insidious neurotoxic substance in gasolines that over a period of time may have an adverse impact on the health of our children if continued exposure is allowed to exist.
I want to be very clear on this matter. This is taken in and accumulates in the body over a long period of time and the outcome of this will not be known for years to come, long after these infants have grown up.
I should also put on the record that this material has been banned in the United States since 1978.
Therefore, if this government is seriously maintaining that increased tobacco taxes are a health measure, then I ask them to move immediately to ban MMT from gasolines in Canada.
The medical evidence continues to accumulate. The substance I speak about, MMT, has to be dealt with very quickly if we are going to protect the lives and health of our nation's children.
As I look across the country and see the alternatives for those engaged in agriculture continuing to diminish, I have to ask this government to stop and examine where it is going and to make sure that those farmers who do wish to take advantage of the REDUX program are given an opportunity through continued funding to get into other areas of production that is acceptable to society and will not affect the health of this nation.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Lambton- Middlesex for his intervention earlier in this House today when he voted against this bill on behalf of his tobacco farmers. He was willing to stand up for them on this, as he has stood up for fanners across this country, not only when he was Minister of Agriculture but since then when he has led this party in the debate in the House of Commons regarding the GATT and the effects on our supply managed commodities.
I spoke earlier in the day on this bill. Madam Speaker, I want to let you know that I will not be repeating what I was saying earlier. What I want to point out to this House before we wind up the debate is the impact this legislation has on our fanning communities, especially the farming communities in my area of Haldimand- Norfolk.
When a government puts on a tax such as this, a burdensome tax that in my belief and in the belief of many people throughout Canada is something that is just a tax grab, unfortunately the impact of that on people in their day to day lives does not seem to come up as often as we might want to expect.
What I have here are some letters from some of my constituents outlining the impacts that this taxation and excessive taxation have on their lives as tobacco farmers. I want to read from a few of these because I think it is important that the House understands, that this government understands, the impacts that some of the decisions have on common people.
I will not reveal any names, but I want to read this letter which outlines the real impact that the taxation has on this one farm family. It states: "My husband and I purchased the farm in 1974 for $140,000 with rights to 37 acres. We had good crops every year and slowly built up our farm from our profits. We bought other rights. All this was possible because of the money we made from our crops. Unfortunately, in 1981 my husband passed away. I was 38 years old with four children. I did not want to sell the farm because I was considering my children's future. When my husband passed away we owed $30,000 because of the blue mould program".
This is just one of the problems, the blue mould problem, faced by tobacco fanners, a disease affecting their crop. These are problems that Canadians in a day to day life do not understand that farmers face. Cana-
Govemment Orders
dians on a day to day basis look out and see either a sunny day or a rainy day. They feel either they can go down to the beach or cannot go down to the beach.
Unfortunately, for the farmer it depends on what the day is like, whether he is going to have a proper crop and whether he can actually survive. If we do not get the amount of sun, if we do not get the amount of rain as required, not only in tobacco but other crops, it makes it difficult for farmers just to get by.
The letter states further: "In 1986 I grew 20 acres of tobacco with my children with an operating loan from the bank. The farm at that time was valued at $850,000. Now it is valued at $125,000".
Just over a few short years the value of that farm fell. What Canadian business person could go on after a business such as that loses the value that it did? This person is directly relating that to excessive taxation.
She goes on to say: "I have had a hard time making my living off of $350 a week. I am writing you this letter to make you realize how hard life is after I have sold my quota. Sometimes I feel like I'm going to have a nervous breakdown.
Even my children are suffering. They are nervous because they see all my hardships and problems. Last year, my 19-year old son underwent terrible surgery for a bleeding ulcer and the specialist says he could not understand how such a young person could get a bleeding ulcer. Without surgery, my son would have died".
The letter goes on to say that the doctor felt that this was a direct result of the stress that had been created within that family because of the troubles that it was having in the farming sector.
Another one I have here is from another family regarding the question of whether the decisions made by the government with regard to excessive taxation have actually been constitutional. He feels that they are against the Charter of Rights. He says: "What happened to the Charter of Rights which Canada and the government are supposed to adhere to? Our life as Canadians has definitely been a tremendous struggle. We have been put out of business, not treated as equals to our tobacco neighbours who were lucky enough to be able to wait one day or six months longer than us and therefore get three times the money".


Government Orders
This person is talking about the group of tobacco farmers, a little over 100, who got out before the REDUX program actually came in.
As I am talking about REDUX, I really want to take to task the Minister of State for Finance when he questioned me today on whether I was, I suppose he challenged me, misleading the House on the question of REDUX.
The fact of the matter is that there is no money now in the hands of the farmers for REDUX. The government says that I should know that it is planning to give money for REDUX. The planning or possible promises have been broken by this government in the past as they have by a number of governments.
Tobacco farmers are not satisfied with the promise from the Minister of State for Finance that there is going to be a solution. I know he is having problems now. He is correct when he says that the NDP provincial government is balking on funding.
They are worse than the Tories.

I cannot judge that yet, because I have not really been in long enough.
To continue on, this gentleman says: "We purchased over 123 acres for 179,000 pounds of quota for our farm in 1984 for $600,000. Within four years, our acreage went from 45 acres to 20 acres."
That answers the question for the people who say: Why can tobacco farmers not get into other forms of farming? You cannot farm anything in Canada on 20 acres or 45 acres and make any sort of living.
There are areas in which tobacco farmers have moved, some of the areas are peanuts, melons and a whole wide range of products. Basically, a lot of the markets for those products have already been taken up elsewhere in Canada.
There has been a lot of success by farmers helped by programs by the government such as AEI, Alternative Initiative Programs, and also other government funding to help them move in. There have been some success stories. I am not saying there have not been.
Unfortunately, now it has cancelled that program.
It has cancelled the Alternative Enterprise Initiative and the government has not given any indication at all that it plans to bring that initiative back.

It has given a commitment because Bob Rae did give a commitment during the election campaign that he would fairly compensate farmers. Unfortunately, this has not come to task yet, but I hope that within the short term the provincial government will get involved in this REDUX program if there is funding from the government. I hope too that it will be able to provide some answers for our tobacco farmers.
Again, we have had promises. We have had the Minister of Finance, the former Minister of Agriculture, come right through my riding, the riding of Elgin and Oxford, and make a commitment prior to the last election that he would help the tobacco industiy. Unfortunately, in my mind and in the mind of most tobacco farmers, they do not feel that that help has been forthcoming.
As I said before, promises have been broken. Also, governments have gone on their own in programs to assist farmers and to assist other industries without provincial involvement.
I would call upon the government and the minister of state because he knows he has the power to do this on his own. If the provincial government goes back on its word to help compensate tobacco farmers, I would expect that the federal government here would go along on it. I would hope that my hon. friends on the government side from tobacco producing areas would be making that point to the government.
I mentioned earlier in the day a group of over 1,000 farmers who banded together and who have put a suit forward to sue the federal and provincial governments for what they say is excessive taxation. They say they have been damaged by this and are asking recourse from both the federal and Ontario provincial governments.
Unfortunately, both governments decided at that time that they would challenge this court decision. Unfortunately for them and fortunately for tobacco farmers, they lost out on that challenge. The judge decided that yes, the tobacco farmers did have a right to sue the government on that fact and that is going on now.



This is a letter from the president of that group of tobacco farmers. It is a fair compensation group. He writes that there is no rationale, no sense of impact and no provision for compensation for those affected by this and previous excesses in government taxation. The only clue we have is a statement from the Minister of Finance on budget day, February 26, 1991, that the huge tax increase was intended to reduce tobacco use and if that tax produced a net revenue decline it was the kind of revenue erosion he would be pleased to accommodate. It says, as stated by the finance minister, it is a tax increase to reduce consumption of tobacco which will result in the item not being purchased and no tax being paid. He says this is illogical. There is no regard for personal liberty. Of about one-third of adult Canadians who enjoy tobacco, a legal product, it has ignored their millions of protests.
There have been millions of protests. These protests have gone in to the Prime Minister in those little cards that you might have seen in your package of tobacco. Those cards were addressed to the Prime Minister. They called upon the Prime Minister to stop his excessive taxing of tobacco products.
There were well over 3 million to 4 million of these tax cards that went in to the Prime Minister's office. I am sure the Prime Minister would not have read them all, but I hope that he would have at least looked at a few of them to get a sense of the outrage smoking Canadians have to excessive taxation. I am saying excessive taxation because I am sure that a majority of these smokers would be willing to pay fair taxation on their tobacco products. I have no doubt about that.
Look at the situation in the United States. I am sure the Americans have the same concern for their health as does the Canadian government. They feel that some form of taxation on their tobacco products is enough to help deal with the adverse health effects that they find in their country due to smoking. They have nowhere near the amount of taxation on their tobacco products that we do. It leads one to believe that somewhere along the line there is something wrong, that one government is going wrong somewhere if it feels that taxation does stop smoking and stops these adverse impacts on its economy and on our economy.
I would suggest that it is the Canadian government that has gone way overboard. It knows it has gone overboard and the only reason it is continuing to increase taxation on tobacco product is in order to get revenue in
Government Orders
a way that most Canadians would not notice. Only one-quarter of all Canadians, six and a half million or so, smoke. I feel that it is this government's intention to continue to increase this taxation and continue to get its revenues in the future from this increased taxation.
I want to finish there because I have said most of what I really wanted to say on this matter this morning. However I want to leave you with one thought. I feel this government, through this taxation policy and through other policies, is driving Canadian agriculture south of the border because if we do not grow tobacco it is going to be grown anyway and people will continue to smoke.
This government is not going to stop other markets from smoking, other countries in the world. Essentially we will lose the business. Canadians will continue to smoke but they will just get their cigarettes from south of the border. That is just another industry that this government, provincial governments and other Canadian governments have been forcing south of the border.
I thank you for the time, Madam Speaker, and I think that is all on this side from those who were going to speak.

Madam Speaker, I would put a question to the hon. member. I listened very carefully the very convincing arguments of both the member for Sarnia-Lambton and the member for Haldimand-Norfolk on behalf of their constituents. The plight of those who are tobacco farmers is certainly not missed. Quite a number of them find themselves in tragic circumstances.
I intend no partisan comment here but I am confused. I would think the House favours attempting to reduce or idealistically eliminate the use of tobacco. The government has argued that one of the quickest and most efficient ways of doing it is by increasing the tax to make the cost prohibitive. The argument on the other side of the House is that, yes, we agree with the objectives of the bill, but if it is anything other than a cash grab give us a signal. Let us give relief to suffering tobacco farmers who find themselves in this predicament through no fault of their own. Let us put some of that tax grab money, until it is used in some fashion that signals good intent, into helping people get off the product. Let us help farmers. Let us help workers trapped innocently in the production thing. Let us help people get off it in whatever way we can: time off work and compensation for the cost of the programs.


Government Orders
There are two messages that seem to be coming in the defence of the tobacco farmer. First, they grow a very fine product. I think that signal sends out a mixed message that maybe this House and the two speakers did not intend. I recall the comments of the Philip Morris company marketing executive who when speaking to a sales group said: "Look, let's understand one thing. We sell a drug. We are not selling tobacco or we are not selling smoking. That is just one method by which this drug is administered and it is a very powerful drug". To make an argument, I think it could easily be misunderstood by the population to say that we make the best drug available.
If I understand the will of the House, it is that we want to do something clearly for the tobacco farmers to ease this enormous burden that came upon them, without the problem that I think both of the previous speakers have articulated very clearly. But the second thing is that we want some of that cash tax grab put into relieving the burden in a committed way, and arguments have been made that that should be cost shared by Ontario. The health care system will be the beneficiary. Canadians will be the beneficiary.
I wonder if the comment on the fact that Canadians make the best tobacco should be clarified that it should not be allowed to continue on that basis. As for the other argument that somehow the additives to gasoline were a serious health problem, that is acknowledged. There is no contest on it. The health minister basically said in one of his reports that lifestyle changes had to be made. It was the surest way to change the health care system. Motor vehicles, tobacco and alcohol were causing tremendous lifestyle drains.
To make an argument that we should not move on tobacco unless we move on the motor vehicles seems again to be moving us away from the critical point that this House basically backs what the government has done. The government, in a show of good faith, should reciprocate by clearly and strongly addressing the problems those farmers face, that the workers in the production and distribution face, and that Canadians face trying to get off tobacco.
I wonder if that might be clarified by the previous speaker.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for North Island-Powell River for his question. I listened intently. It was a little bit confusing near the end. I was not really quite sure whether you were asking if I supported the banning of tobacco totally as an illegal drug and thereby there should be compensation for farmers once it was banned. I believe you will find that most tobacco farmers would be just as happy if the product was banned altogether and they were compensated for doing that.
In terms of what my hon. friend for Lambton- Middlesex said earlier, the point he was trying to make was that the government was being-and I do not want to put words in his mouth-somewhat hypocritical by claiming on the one hand to be doing something for the health of Canadians by taxing a legal product and on the other hand doing nothing to ban the use of MMT as an additive. I would agree with him. I believe these are areas that the government should continue to look at.
The point being made by my hon. friend for Lamb-ton-Middlesex is that there are a number of these products used within Canada. In the last few days he said that during the free trade debate there was a promise by this government that there would be a level playing field, that Canadian farmers would be able to use certain products that American farmers were able to use.
The practice in Canada is that we ban products, one of which is MMT. We ban other pesticides and other herbicides in Canada and say we cannot have them on our products. Then we import them from other countries including the United States.
The point my hon. friend for Lambton-Middlesex has been trying to make is that we should have a level playing field and that Canadian farmers should have the same access to these products as do Americans. It is hypocritical of the government to claim on the one hand to be doing something for the health of Canadians by overtaxing tobacco and on the other hand doing nothing to ban the use of MMT which, as he says, is a real danger especially to the health of young Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is truly convoluted and a little difficult to follow, but I think from the careful explanation of the previous speaker that both he and the member for Lamb ton- Middlesex do in fact support the initiatives of the government that would lead to a reduction in the use of tobacco in Canada. They make a very strong argument that farmers should be compensated. I guess by extension others should be compensated as well for losses through the support of this House of the government's initiative to increase taxes on tobacco.
Madam Speaker, I am not quite sure that I follow the hon. member. I guess my point is that this government has been unfairly taxing tobacco products in Canada.
It is unfairly taxing everybody.

"It is unfairly taxing everybody", as my hon. friend says. This is nothing but another tax grab by the government, and Canadians are really fed up with paying such high taxes. This is nothing more than a tax grab. Canadians will let this government know at the end of things, in the next election, what they feel about these high undue taxes.
