speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the very brief time I have tonight I would like to raise on the adjournment motion a question that I put to the government, in particular to the minister of trade, on June 10, 1991. It was on a very important issue of concern to the country and in particular to my home province of British Columbia and my riding including the Prince George and northern interior area of the province. It was in regard to the softwood lumber tariff memorandum of understanding.
I guess it is a good example of how the world does change. At that time the issue that was very important to us was the thousands of jobs that were being lost in the forest industry basically because this government, along with the former Social Credit government in British Columbia, signed an agreement essentially with the Americans that allowed the imposition of a tariff on softwood lumber products from Canada into the United States.
At the time my question was put to the government to see what it was doing to tell Washington, D.C. that Canada wanted to manage its forests on its own.
Subsequent to that the government moved on September 3, 1991 to terminate the softwood lumber agreement with the U.S., which at the time I applauded with some reservations. Of course the reservations were such that it had taken some time and many thousands of jobs had been lost in the meantime.
In going in to some new negotiations, what assurances could the government give us that it would stand firm and would not sign another deal like it did in the later part of 1986?
That is essentially the stage we are at now. To whoever is going to respond on the government side, I think there are two points I would especially like to hear tonight. The first is an assurance that the government can give, in having the ongoing discussions on this issue with Washington, D.C., that it will not cave in like it did under the previous provincial government and this government. Second, I would like some detail on the assurances the Minister of International Trade provided to me by way of


Adjournment Debate
letter that any Canadian forest producers would be protected, watched out for or taken care of in light of any threats of retaliation from the United States.
That is what I would like to hear from the government tonight. It is a very important issue for lumber producers across Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canada-United States softwood lumber memorandum of understanding (MOU) was negotiated to avoid the imposition of countervailing duties on exports of Canadian softwood lumber to the United States. The softwood lumber MOU was intended, first, to end a bitter and highly politicized bilateral trade dispute over Canadian lumber exports to the United States, and second, to provide time for Canadian provinces to implement planned changes in provincial forest policies, which included increases in stumpage and other charges to the Canadian industry.
Madam Speaker, conditions have changed significantly since the MOU was signed. A large portion of Canada's softwood lumber exports to the United States are no longer subject to the export charge. The charge has been replaced entirely in British Columbia and partially in Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces are exempt. In all, changes in the application of the MOU's provisions have served to reduce export charge collections for Canada to roughly $40 million from a level of $400 million in 1987, the first year of the MOU.
Madam Speaker, market conditions have also changed since the MOU was signed in 1986. Canada's share of the U.S. market has fallen from a peak of 32.8 per cent in 1985 to 26.8 per cent in 1990, its lowest level in 13 years. The increase in the value of the Canadian dollar, combined with increased log costs to the Canadian industry, have significantly enhanced the competitiveness of U.S. producers compared to Canadian producers.
The memorandum of understanding has therefore served its purpose, and Canada exercised its right to terminate the agreement on October 4. Canada-United States softwood lumber trade can now be put back on a normal basis, subject to the rules of the Free Trade Agreement and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
Madam Speaker, in response to domestic pressure, the U.S. Administration has decided to launch a new countervailing duty case against softwood lumber from Canada and has also imposed an interim border measure requiring importers to post bonds on shipments of lumber from those producers that were subject to the export charge.
The government has objected strongly to this U.S. action and is seeking the immediate establishment of a GATT panel which will be asked to rule on whether the price which a government charges for the right to cut timber is a countervailable subsidy and whether the Section 301 bonding requirement is consistent with U.S. obligations under the GATT.
There is no basis, Madam Speaker, for a countervailing duty investigation. There is no subisdy to Canadian lumber producers. The government will be working closely with the Canadian industry and the provinces in mounting the best possible defence in fighting these allegations of subsidy.
Madam Speaker, in conclusion, Canada is in a better position to fight the U.S. countervail action than we were in 1986. In addition to the changes in provincial stumpage policies and market conditions, Canada now has access to binding dispute-settlement provisions.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to have the four minutes or so available to me to discuss a question that I posed to the government benches on October 4 and 5. It is in regard to the government's lacklustre commitment, or failure to endorse in strong language, the continuation of the success story that has marked the de Havilland Corporation of metropolitan Toronto.
We on this side of the House have tried to convince the government of a number of realities. The first is that de Havilland happens to be the flag ship for our Canadian aerospace industry. It also happens to be the largest single industrial employer in metropolitan Toronto. There are currently some 4,900 workers directly employed at de Havilland, despite the fact that Boeing has announced that starting January 1,300 of these individuals would be laid off. The other important factor is that for every direct job at de Havilland there is approximately four created in the small business sector


which feeds in both contracts and supplies in terms of aerospace parts for de Havilland Corporation.
De Havilland is very crucial economically to metropolitan Toronto and indeed to the province of Ontario and to the country so far as employment in contracts across Canada, including the province of Quebec, in very significant measure, but also the aspect of a federal government being able to promote a national aerospace industry like any other country of the western world.
In response to our questions the minister of industry actually suggested that the ball is in the provincial court. If there is an initiative for assistance and promotion it ought to come from the provincial governments. We find on this side of the House that that is a complete abdication of any national responsibility to support and sustain our aerospace industry.
We have already gone down the path of the Avro Arrow. We know what that did to the industry back then in terms of employment, in terms of research and development, in terms of morale. What we want to avoid is a repeat of history under the same Tory administration in 1991.
What we on this side of the House have been seeking is a clear, unequivocal assurance, not of passing the political buck to the provinces or the municipalities but clearly to say to the people of Canada that the federal government will endeavour to continue to support de Havilland. If no private interests come together to assist de Havilland, then this federal government must certainly carry out its responsibilities to the fullest to ensure that jobs, that research and that technology related to the aerospace industry remains in Canada for Canadians.
I am looking forward to the answer from the government benches this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to start by pointing out that the aerospace industry in Canada is a highly significant component of Canada's industrial base employing 64,000
Adjournment Debate
and generating $8 billion in sales, of which $6 billion is exports.

Canada's aerospace industry has performed better than other companies throughout the world even if it has been performing in a highly competitive environment. The reason is that the aerospace industry in Canada counts on sales of about 30 per cent to the military while it is not the case in other countries throughout the world.

This government recognizes the aerospace industry not only for its economic benefits but also as an engine for technology development with spin-off benefits for other domestic industries. To this end, Industry Science and Technology Canada has for years supported, and continues to support, the R&D activities of the industry through cost-sharing in the range of 30 per cent to 50 per cent, which is generally repayable through royalties.

De Havilland in its early years after privatization achieved considerable market recognition and success with the Dash 8 product line. Now there are 286 Dash 8 aircraft operating world-wide as compared to 20 in early 1986. I fly in one every week coming and going to my riding.
De Havilland received support from Industry, Science and Technology to develop and enhance the Dash 8 product line which improved the technical attributes and attractiveness of the product.
Boeing decided to sell its interest in the company in 1990 and shortly thereafter the economic recession and dramatic downturn in airline travel resulted in a severe slump in demand for commuter aircraft. The effect of the slump was a weakening of de Havilland's order book which may necessitate production rate cutbacks as we know involving employee reductions. We are confident that with the upturn in the economy de Havilland will regain its place as a high technology company and as a dynamic enterprise that will continue to provide a major economic impact in the Toronto area and also on the Canadian industry scene.


Adjournment Debate
We feel confident that de Havilland can bounce back and the government is prepared and committed to support any moves that are made in order to maintain de Havilland as a effective and strong company.

Madam Speaker, a few weeks ago, on September 24,1 asked the Minister of Agriculture a question on joint plans for the Canadian dairy producers. I got an answer from the Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture. It was far from satisfactory anyway.
Basically, the problem is that dairy producers in Quebec have decided that it is extremely important that production costs be included in the formula according to which the actual production costs of 70 per cent of the most productive farmers be used as a basis or basic criterion applied to all Quebec dairy producers.
There seems to be a concern within the Quebec farmers union, and rightly so, since the advisory committee has learned through the office of the Minister of Agriculture that the rate of $43 per hundred weight of milk was going to drop by about 5 per cent.
In other words, our farm producers, particularly our dairy producers, are under pressure because of this drop in the hundredweight price. At present, a farmer with 35 to 45 dairy cows earns around $26,000 a year. This is not much, as you know. In fact, that is barely more than minimum wage if you factor in all their hours of work.
What are the Quebec farmers and dairy producers most concerned about? They are concerned about the pressures exerted, and this must be pointed out, by the Agriculture Department to take into account the US daily production, the world cheese price and maybe other factors, so that the price of milk in Canada may drop by 5 per cent. You cannot operate that way. We have a supply management system which has proven very beneficial. Quotas are valuable because we have a fair and equitable system to maintain milk prices, and dairy producers who abused the system were penalized, as we know.
That is why basically our fanners are worried about these negotiations, and rightfully so. When we look at dairy production in Canada since we know that 48 per
cent of it comes from Quebec, its 13,500 producers, they have every reason to be concerned. This sector of the agri-food industry is very important for us. Madam Speaker, I would like to reassure them through the hon. parliamentary secretary, if he could deal with the criteria applicable to dairy production.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to respond to the concerns the hon. member has just raised.
In particular, with regard to the pricing of milk, about two and a half or three years ago there was a dairy task force that was established by the then Minister of Agriculture, the present Minister of Finance, to try to make sure that we keep a very competitive up-to-date dairy industry in this country. Whether it was in Quebec or any other province, it would not matter, it would make sure that it is a competitive industry across this nation.
Our consumers and the people of Canada have become very used to a good quality, wholesome product which we expect and should expect. They have met that standard. They have met the challenge of doing that. They have provided very, very good products to us.
Pricing of the product has been taken over through a recommendation by the task force. The government does not set the prices for that milk as I understand it today, if I understand the member's question properly.
I know this past summer the pricing of milk was changed from a different way of measuring the fat content or the skim milk part of the product to a different system. If there has been any reduction it would be because of the different way of pricing but fair, I believe, right across the country.
The most important thing is the negotiations we believe that are taking place at the GATT because this is where article XI allows us to control imports of dairy products into this country, and poultry products as well. This is very important to us, and we are vigorously supporting article XI. We have support from other nations around the world, but that is a very strong and important element to the continuation of our supply managed sector.


Our position has not changed since it was developed and has remained steadfast. We hope that with that and with all the stakeholders being involved we will give the dairy producers the confidence they need to continue the fine work they have been doing.

Madam Speaker, in September I had asked the minister of housing, and the parliamentary secretary got up and answered, my simple question: When is the government going to introduce its 5 per cent down payment for new home buyers?
The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has had a proposal before this government that would reduce that insurable limit of a home's value to 95 per cent. Currently we have a minimum of 10 per cent down payment which is required for a mortgage. The proposal that the government has been studying, and has before it, is one that would call for a 5 per cent down payment. It is supported by everyone from the Canadian Real Estate Association, Canadian Home Builders, to the potential new home buyer. Everyone is supporting this proposal except this government.
I think the federal government has failed to understand the importance of what the recession has done to the housing sector. Hundreds of thousands of construction workers have been laid off and construction companies have even gone bankrupt. Surplus inventories in new houses will ensure that the new work will be slow in coming and the supply of materials and workers will shrink continually as the recession lingers and consumer confidence remains low.
A 5 per cent down payment is a tried and true mechanism that will encourage housing construction and the 95 per cent NHA insured mortgages were the benchmark financing mechanism between 1960 and 1982.
A study by CMHC indicates that a 5 per cent down payment would open up the housing market to some
200,000	families. About 10,000 to 15,000 this year alone would be able to take advantage of this new proposal.
Adjournment Debate
Studies have also indicated that in the current economic environment the lower down payment would result in only marginal and easily manageable risk to the mortgage insurance fund managed by CMHC.
In other words, there would be no cost to the treasury.
The recent stability of housing prices and the decline in interest rates make it an ideal time to introduce the 5 per cent down payment program. Currently the oversupply of housing, high unemployment in the industry, the stabilizing of high house prices, decrease in interest rates, the fact that it will not cost this government treasury any money, and the 5 per cent down payment should provide a stimulus to the housing sector which is so badly needed.
The government in its answer to my question in September said that simply lower interest rates would be enough to bring the buyers back into the market. That simply is not going to be enough. The housing industry now is faced with an interesting dilemma. Consumers are waiting for this announcement. The word has been out that the government will announce it soon and therefore there has been a hesitancy on the part of home buyers to want to purchase that home. The government needs to answer the industry's claim that the time has come for this 5 per cent down payment and it can finally announce this program so that it can get on with putting people back to work, putting people in new homes, and essentially getting people off the unemployment roles.
I would again urge and ask this government if it is prepared to announce today the initiation of the 5 per cent down payment for first time home buyers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question concerning the creation of housing construction jobs through the introduction of a 5 per cent down payment for first time home buyers.
We have to recognize that today's generation of homeowners often remembers the level of down payment as the single most important obstacle it had to overcome when it purchased its first home.

Adjournment Debate
Many of those who became homeowners in the 1960s and 1970s would not have been able to purchase a home had they been required to provide a down payment of more than 5 per cent.
Ninety-five per cent of the NHA-insured mortgages were the benchmark financing technique from 1960 to 1982.
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is looking at a variety of ways to help Canadians everywhere access home ownership. One possibility is by once again offering a government-backed mortgage insurance for down payments as low as 5 per cent.
CMHC officials estimate that reducing down payments to 5 per cent would allow up to 200,000 Canadian renters with a reasonable opportunity for home ownership. Of these, there could be some 10,000 potential first-time home buyers in the first year.
The support of the Canadian Home Builders Association and its affiliates for 95 per cent NHA mortgage insurance is very much appreciated. CMHC recognizes that the home building industry is a vital factor in the Canadian economy providing jobs for many skilled tradespeople.
CMHC is encouraged to note that on a national basis housing starts are expected to rise 21 per cent to 178,000 units in 1992.
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation wants to help first-time home buyers weigh all their options and make sound decisions. Ninety-five per cent mortgage financing is certainly one of the options being considered.
We will be pleased to advise this House and the hon. member as soon as a decision has been reached on this important matter.

Madam Speaker, today in The Toronto Star a report was published on the preoccupation in the mind of municipal voters in metro Toronto. From that study, we learn that the most important problem in the mind of municipal electors on metropolitan Toronto is crime, law and order to an astonishing degree where it peaks in the city of Scarborough, and to a very close second, I believe, in the city of Toronto.
Evidently we have here a preoccupation that is deeply felt in the heart of every neighbourhood across the city.
This brings me then to the issue of illicit drugs and the anti-drug enforcement which in the past five weeks I have raised in this House by way of a Standing Order and then by way of a question of the Solicitor General who sought to give me quite an encouraging answer on September 24. At that time, to my question as to whether the federal government would refund or return a share of the funds seized by the RCMP in drug arrests, the answer by the Solicitor General was that he knew that this bond had been made previously by various police officials and mayors across the country and that he, having acknowledged that this is a valid point, would look into this matter. I am quoting here from page 2636 of Hansard'.
-we are looking at the possibility of returning funds spent on
investigations to the various jurisdictions.
The Solicitor General went on to comment on the fact that the National Drug Strategy announced by the Prime Minister is a five year preoccupation which expires in 1992. While we appreciate the complexity and the difficulty of this issue, even the best friends of the Prime Minister could not claim that this National Drug Strategy has been a resounding success. In the last four years the issue has deteriorated and, as shown in this survey conducted by The Toronto Star, it is now so deeply felt that it tops the polls, so to say, in metro Toronto. I suspect that this is not an isolated occurrence. In conclusion, I would ask the parliamentary secretary whether she could tell us when the minister will make a decision on this request made by politicians of all parties in this House, I presume, and also by mayors and reeves across the country on returning a portion of the funds that accrue from certain RCMP initiatives to which the various police forces have contributed as well in the course of their investigations and seizures and the like. Also does the government have a specific plan in mind to strengthen the national drug strategy which, at the present time, seems to be rather weakly implemented when it comes to the regional and the local level.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to start by thanking the hon. member for Davenport for his particular interest in public safety. He is, of course, concerned about an article expressing the concerns of the people of Toronto, but I think every memberof this House would agree that these concerns are shared by all Canadians.

A number of police forces, particularly in Metro Toronto, have been calling for the return of a portion of the assets forfeited as a result of their investigations. It is suggested that these forfeited funds could be used to enhance their drug demand reduction activities through education, and prevention.
The Solicitor General fully supports the balance of supply and demand reduction efforts by the police. Police forces across Canada have done an exceptional job in this respect, and I am confident that they will continue to do so. I am also aware that many departments are feeling the effects of fiscal restraint. They must do more with less. To their credit, by working smarter, police forces have met this challenge well.
Proceeds of crime investigations can be costly. The recovery of forfeited proceeds is certainly one possible way to finance these complex and time-consuming investigations. However, careful consideration must be given to the question of whether asset sharing can be implemented without jeopardizing the impartial administration of the criminal justice system and the delivery of
Adjournment Debate
policing services in particular. This issue is being reviewed by the Department of Justice.
In the interim, as a partner in Canada's Drug Strategy, the Ministry of the Solicitor General will continue to work with police departments across Canada to reduce supply and demand for drugs. Federal dollars will continue to be used to assist police at all levels through contributions to research and development.
Specifically in the area of proceeds of crime legislation introduced under the Strategy, the Ministry of the Solicitor General, in consultation with the RCMP, is exploring ways to facilitate co-operation in anti-drug profiteering law enforcement. The ultimate goal of these efforts is to address the difficulties created by the time and labour intensive nature of proceeds investigations and to encourage the participation of all police forces.
